item.title: Aaron Rodgers rips Steelers coach Mike McCarthy, says he fell asleep in team meeting and he learned of benching from Pat Freiermuth
item.description: Rodgers appeared on the Pat McAfee Show after the team announced his benching Tuesday night.
item.content:encoded:
Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers did not stay silent for long following his surprise benching, which was announced by the team on Tuesday night.

The three-time MVP joined the Pat McAfee Show on Wednesday afternoon to address his benching … and he did not hold back when it came to sharing his side of how the events of the week unfolded — or when it comes to his feelings about head coach Mike McCarthy.

“I found out that I was gonna be inactive on a phone call last night from Pat Freiermuth,” Rodgers stated. “I was talking to Muth and a couple of the guys, and he said, ‘I can’t believe they’re doing this.’ And I said, ‘Doing what?’ I didn’t know. And he told me, and obviously, there had been a lot of things in motion at that point. I didn’t hear from Mike [McCarthy].”

“Mike and I talked for a long time the last few days, and that word [benching] never came up,” Rodgers continued.

After that, Rodgers released a total windfall of scathing accusations against McCarthy, ripping into his head coach for a series of bizarre events over the past week that “ultimately led to where we’re at now.”

Rodgers highlights bizarre sequence of events with McCarthy leading up to benching

On Wednesday, Rodgers stated that McCarthy arrived late to a quarterbacks meeting, in which he fell asleep and was snoring. Then, on Thursday, Rodgers accused McCarthy of missing an offensive meeting. On Friday, Rodgers said McCarthy missed the walkthrough.

“Doesn’t come to the first walkthrough. Doesn’t come to the protection walkthrough on Thursday. Saturday, he misses the morning meeting, and we don’t have a team meeting Saturday night for whatever reason in Philly. And then comes Sunday, when obviously we struggled, and the product wasn’t great.”

‘Mike [McCarthy] didn’t want to get to know the defense’

Rodgers also ripped into McCarthy's relationships with players on the team, alleging that he didn't care to get to know the defense and had lost many of those players well before the end.

“There were some guys early on that were … didn’t like the way things were going, especially defensive guys. Mike didn’t want to get to know the defense,” Rodgers said. “At one point, I told him, ‘You should really lean into the defensive guys a little bit more and talk to those guys,’ and he said, ‘Well, I don’t think I need to.’ And I said, ‘Well, I disagree with that.’”

“He already kind of lost a lot of those guys, and I think the nail in the coffin for so many of us was, at halftime, toward the end of it … He says, ‘Alright, 1-2-3-Packers!’ That’s what he broke it down on in the locker room,” Rodgers said. “We all looked around, going, ‘What the f***? What is going on? Where’s his head at, at this point?”

Week 12 TE Rankings

1. Trey McBride (vs. WAS) - 60.5 proj. yards

McBride is going to be just fine. Josh Johnson was a checkdown artist all Week 11 against the Chiefs, and McBride was still trying to hurdle defenders and work his butt off. The Cardinals have nowhere else to go in the pass game, and they're going to be in huge negative scripts the rest of the way. He'll lead the position in targets by a comfortable margin. Touchdowns will be hard to come by, but that's okay.

The matchup is great. The Commanders will blitz and leave underneath gaps behind it for McBride. Washington has allowed the second-most fantasy points to TEs, including 77 yards to Mike Gesicki on Monday Night Football. Isaiah Likely has been the TE1 overall in each of his games against them. It's the same role in the offense here.

2. Colston Loveland (at DET) - 52.5 proj. yards

Loveland is the TE5 on TE4 usage since Caleb Williams returned in Week 6. He's averaging 7.5 targets over the past month and hurdled a defender for a score last week as a full-time player.

This is a great matchup for Loveland. The Bears project for the third-most points, and the Lions are without LB Jack Campbell amongst others. They've allowed the most half PPR points to the position (17.4 per game), and Loveland had 91-1 against them in Week 18 of last year himself.

3. Isaiah Likely (at IND) - 50.5 proj. yards

Likely is the TE2 on TE3 overall this year, averaging 8.1 targets per game despite largely leading games. He's simply that important to the offense, essentially operating as a bigger Wan'Dale Robinson. Last week's dud was defense- and game-script related. I'm not worried about it.

The Colts are tanking and have been shredded due to inexperienced LB play. The Giants travel as 6.5-point road favorites, carrying a 24-point implied team total (10th). It's a good spot for Likely.

4. T.J. Hockenson (vs. ATL) - 44.5 proj. yards

Hockenson is benefiting from the Kirk Cousins trade and the Jordan Addison injury. He is the TE8 on TE6 usage over his last four games, seeing between 7.6 and 10.1 expected half PPR points in all four contests. He's a stable low-end TE1 option.

Atlanta ranks 14th in half PPR points allowed to tight ends at 10.9 points per game. It’s been better against the position of late, but it’s without FS Jessie Bates now. Minnesota enters as 7-point home favorites with an implied team total of 24.25 points (eighth).

5. Brock Bowers (at CLE)

We'll see how much he practices here.

6. George Kittle (vs. SEA) - 46.5 proj. yards

Kittle is the TE4 on TE4 usage this season. His involvement could take a slight hit with Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel Sr. healthy and Keenan Allen added to the lineup, but there are few with more big-play ability, despite being 33 years old coming off a torn Achilles. Just ask the Vikings, who were TE eliminators before Kittle finished as the TE2 overall with a pair of scores. Incredible.

Seattle ranks 27th in half PPR points allowed to tight ends at 8.1 per game, though they did give up 65 yards to Colston Loveland in Week 8. Kittle has had less luck against them, finishing with 24, 29 and 25 yards in his games, respectively, since S/LB Nick Emmanwori showed up. San Francisco enters as 3-point home favorites with a 25.25-point implied team total (eighth). It's a tough spot for Kittle. I'm just not going to ever doubt him.

7. Harold Fannin Jr. (vs. LV) - 49.5 proj. yards

Fannin ranks as the TE2 on TE4 usage over his last four games, the best stretch of his sophomore season. Coach Todd Monken has recently stated that they have to keep him very involved after not throwing him a screen for the first six weeks of the year. Bizarre! He still has some of the best YAC moments in the NFL, not at his position. All positions. Fannin has drawn at least nine targets in three of his last four outings. What a star.

The Raiders present a generous spot, ranking fifth in half PPR points allowed to tight ends with 13.4 per game. Las Vegas conceded 74 yards on eight targets to Evan Engram (!!!) last week, along with a 4-catch, 58-yard finish to George Kittle in Week 9. Cleveland enters the matchup as 4.5-point home favorites with an implied team total of 23 points (15th).

8. Travis Kelce (at BUF) - 46.5 proj. yards

Kelce sits as the TE3 on TE8 usage over his last four games, averaging 12.7 half PPR points on 8.4 expected points per game. He bounced back from a 2-target outing in Week 10 with a season-high 22.4 half PPR points against Arizona in Week 11, catching 6-of-7 targets for 74 yards and two touchdowns alongside a season-high 58 air yards.

The Bills are a good matchup for Kelce, not because they are a bad defense. It's that they are better at stopping the run than the pass, and because the Chiefs are actually underdogs. More dropbacks than normal wouldn't be a surprise, and the weather calls for some rain and wind, likely meaning more underneath passes than anything deep. Kelce has 66, 19, 8, 75, 83 and 112 yards, respectively, against Buffalo since 2022, for what it's worth. Kansas City heads on the road as 3-point road underdogs with an implied team total of 23.75 points (11th). He'll see SS Cole Bishop in the box plenty. It'll be an even matchup there.

9. Sam LaPorta (vs. CHI) - 44.5 proj. yards

It's been a quiet year for LaPorta, but he was able to find space a couple of times against the Bucs for explosives, finishing as the TE12 on TE8 usage. Across the year, he's the TE7 on TE5 usage, though most of that came before Week 6. He's only the TE29 on TE11 usage this past month. With all Lions, it's best to take the largest sample. There are more mouths than targets to go around, so somebody will get left behind at times. He can get hot at any time.

Chicago ranks 24th in half PPR points allowed to opposing tight ends, yielding 8.7 points per game. Across their last three games with DT Jeffery Simmons in-house, the Bears have given up 4.5 points or fewer to opposing TE rooms, though that's the Saints, Bucs and Seahawks. LaPorta has been the TE31, TE5 and TE8 against them most recently. Detroit enters as 2.5-point home underdogs with an implied team total of 26.5 points (sixth). He'll need a touchdown to pay off.

10. Brenton Strange (vs. TEN) - 32.5 proj. yards

The volume is not there (4.2 targets per game), but Strange is a TD threat at any moment. With the Titans tanking, it's a great spot to hope for a score or two. The Jaguars project for 31.0 points. Tennessee has allowed 361.8 passing yards per game this month. That boggles the mind. Strange has also been the TE11, TE5 and TE5 against them most recently.

11. Dalton Kincaid (vs. KC) - 40.5 proj. yards

Kincaid said he's playing, but he's only been limited with thumb and ankle injuries on the official report. He's likely not fully healthy, but this game is big enough to push to play after taking a week off. There will be rainy and windy conditions to fight through, so there's a really low floor just if they want to run the ball in heavier sets. His ankle could also be impacted by the sloppy field conditions, too. Kincaid has been the TE9 on TE14 usage this year with no rhyme or reason for when he's going to have a random big game. I'd love to hear Kincaid theories if you have them!

Kansas City's defense represents a run-funnel tendency, as opponents have thrown on just 46% of neutral plays against them, the lowest in the NFL. That said, when teams pass, the ball can get funneled to TEs. They've allowed the seventh-most half PPR points to the position, with both Brock Bowers (TE2 overall) and Trey McBride (TE7) doing their thing recently. Part of it is that they have two stud outside CBs to slow down WRs, while being more mediocre up the spine. Buffalo enters Thanksgiving as 3-point home favorites with an implied total of 26.75 points (fifth). For what it's worth, Kincaid popped off for 101 yards in Week 9 of last year against this defense.

12. Chig Okonkwo (at ARI) - 38.5 proj. yards

13. Tucker Kraft (at LAR) - 37.5 proj. yards

Kraft is a distant third option in the pass game. He's only the TE15 on TE8 usage this season thanks to some untimely drops and a huge regression in the yards after catch department. Predictably so. He's too talented to not have a couple of big games down the stretch, but he's been on the TE1/2 border all year. There's no reason to change that now.

The Rams have been stingy against tight ends, ranking 29th with 8.0 half PPR points allowed per game. They've faced Trey McBride twice (37 and 53 scoreless yards) and Brock Bowers (73 scoreless), too. Green Bay heads into the matchup as 3-point road underdogs carrying an implied team total of 20.75 points (19th).

14. Tyler Higbee (vs. GB) - 29.5 proj. yards

Higbee is a nice streaming option for those in TE trouble. The Rams used formations rarely used in Week 10 without their top-2 WRs, but we'll see if they stick with those after the bye in a game expected to be a lot closer than the Cardinals blowout. It'd make sense for the Rams to use plenty of 3-TE looks, and Higbee is the loosest athlete of the bunch when in them. Even as a part-time player in Week 10, Higbee had four targets on nine routes. Two of them were in the end zone on first-read looks. I think there's more upside here than what his recent box scores would suggest.

The Packers have been very good at defending TEs for a couple of reasons. One: they have awesome safeties; two: they have a lot of chaotic pre-snap looks that sometimes keep TEs in to block. The Rams are more equipped to beat them, especially with a bye week to prepare.

15. Tyler Warren (vs. NYG) - 27.5 proj. yards

Warren is not making enough plays in the pass game. He's not a loose athlete, rather trying to overpower or win in a straight line. That's a missing trait versus the truly elite TEs across the league. He's more of a Diet Coke Tucker Kraft than a Trey McBride type. His situation is getting harder to trust, too, with Anthony Richardson Sr. stepping into the starting lineup. We seriously don't even know how well he can see!!! He's also a threat to steal goal-line scores and wants to launch the ball well over the head of Warren's typical target depth. Happy Turkey Week, everyone. It’s become Turkey Week because the NFL seems unable to stop expanding its schedule around the holiday. Football kicks off early on Wednesday night with the Packers and Rams, a game that is crucial for both teams in order to stay afloat in their respective divisions.

That’s a theme across much of the week, with a lot of teams seeing Week 12 as critical for their chances. Monday Night Football between the Panthers and Buccaneers could settle the NFC South, the Bears and Lions could battle for control of the NFC North on Thanksgiving, and Raiders vs. Browns could help decide a Wild Card spot in the AFC.

Let’s dive into this week’s games.

item.title: Aaron Rodgers claims Mike McCarthy fell asleep in meetings
item.description: Aaron Rodgers claims Mike McCarthy fell asleep in team meetings.
item.content:encoded:
The Pittsburgh Steelers made the stunning decision late last night to bench their veteran quarterback Aaron Rodgers. The decision came as a shock to many and is believed to be wildly unpopular in the Steelers locker room.

Appearing on The Pat McAfee Show, the legendary quarterback broke his silence on the decision and made a stunning claim about Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy.

“Last Wednesday, we were in a quarterback meeting,” Rodgers said. “Mike came in late, sat down, and when the 10 minutes began snoring. Woke up, was rattling his papers. We all looked around. Five minutes later, you hear the snoring again.  And less than five minutes after that, he walks out of the room.”

Rodgers went on to say that McCarthy constantly misses walkthroughs and had admitted to being behind on film on several occasions. The quarterback admitted that even general manager Omar Khan is aware of McCarthy’s sleeping habits inside the facility.

It’s safe to say that Rodgers has played his final down with the Steelers, and quite possibly his career. This situation has been blown wide open and is far from over. The veteran quarterback believes his head coach was out to get him, and McCarthy still believes Rodgers got him fired from the Packers in 2018. The relationship that originally brought Rodgers back to the Steelers for another year is now the reason the Steelers’ season has gone off the rails.

Let us know what you think in the comments. Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more!

item.title: Rams break out new 20 personnel package ahead of Packers game
item.description: Breaking down the Rams newest personnel package that the Packers are sure to see tonight.
item.content:encoded:
Sean McVay has made a habit of turning injuries into new ideas. Last season, when injuries hit the Los Angeles Rams’ wide receivers, he leaned heavily on 13 personnel, using three tight ends to keep the offense moving.

This year, injuries have hit both receiver and tight end, and McVay’s answer is a 20 personnel package with two running backs, no tight ends and three receivers. Players said it wasn’t installed until the Monday before the Rams’ week 10 game, but they still had 17 plays in the “Pony” package ready by the following Sunday, and they covered a lot of ground.

“Pony” personnel is two running backs instead of the traditional running back/fullback combination. 20 personnel is two backs, zero tight ends, three wide receivers. In the diagram above, there are no tight ends.

The package is a good example of the “illusion of complexity.” Most of the calls were designed passes, and with only three vertical threats at the snap, it shouldn’t have stressed a defense much on paper. In practice, it did. Between the motion, the split-back alignment and a variety of protections, defenders had to account for the entire field on almost every snap.

The package started with a run-pass option. Kyren Williams motioned out of the backfield on a bubble route, and the defense didn’t adjust in time. That gave the quarterback an easy choice.

On one side, two receivers were blocking two defensive backs for Williams in space. On the other, he would have been handing off into a seven-man box with only five blockers. The ball went outside, as it should have.

If the Rams develop a run game in this package, this is a natural place to start. The run side is mid zone, a scheme the line has blocked for years, and the bubble gives the defense a reason to stay honest.

The second play was a staple Rams passing concept, a variant of their corner-choice concept. Since Williams is one of the best running backs in the NFL at running choice routes, here he is given a two-way go and reads the defender over him and breaks inside or outside based on leverage. He can also sit the route down between the zone defenders.

Normally, sending the back out on that route means giving up a blocker. From split backs, though, the second back stays in, so the Rams keep six-man protection while Williams runs the route. It ended up as a drop but expect to see this one again.

Later on, the Rams came back to the same concept but flipped. This time, the Cardinals were playing split safety cover-6 with cover-2 to the backside to take away the choice route underneath. Stafford saw this and threw the vertical route hole shot into the cover-2 void between the corner and safety.

Another passing variant they can run from this formation is the stick/flat/mini dagger concept. This play design is a design the Packers love to run as well.

Stafford hit a no-look throw here to the crossing route on the mini dagger side.

The split-back alignment also gives the Rams more flexibility in protection. They can slide six-man protection to either side, depending on where the biggest threat lines up. They can also use their usual double-chip protection in a new way.

Usually, a tight end chips one edge rusher and the back chips the other. With two backs in the backfield, each one can chip the rusher on his side before releasing, which gives deeper routes more time to develop.

When the Rams want more players running routes, they can go to five-man protection and use one of the backs as the flat-control route. Most passing concepts need someone working underneath to the flat, and the backfield is a natural place to run it from. The defense sees two backs, and either one could be blocking, chipping or running a route.

As usual with McVay, there were several screens built off motion. The best was a middle screen behind a flare motion by the running back. When the back released toward the sideline, the cornerback started backing up, and the motion pulled his eyes away from the receiver in front of him.

By the time the receiver caught the ball, an offensive lineman was already coming at the defender, and the screen worked exactly as designed.

What makes the package impressive isn’t just the plays. It’s how quickly it came together. McVay didn’t rebuild his offense to use 20 personnel. He took concepts the Rams already run with other personnel groupings and adapted them to two backs.

The bubble RPO uses the same mid zone the line already knows. The protections follow the same rules with different players. The screens use the same motions the Rams have used for years. It looks new, but it’s built from familiar pieces, and that’s why a package installed on Monday could work on Sunday.

The bigger question is where it goes from here and what will the Packers see. A two-back package with Williams as the main weapon has been a long time coming. If McVay adds a real run game to what he showed this past week, the injuries that forced this change could end up giving the Rams a lasting new wrinkle in their offense.

item.title: Aaron Rodgers: Mike McCarthy fell asleep in meeting last week, broke down Steelers with "1-2-3 Packers"
item.description: Rodgers's first comments since being benched by the Steelers came on The Pat McAfee Show.
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Rodgers made his first public comments since being benched by the Steelers on The Pat McAfee Show on Wednesday afternoon and they were very critical of head coach Mike McCarthy.

Rodgers said he did not hear the news of the quarterback change directly from McCarthy or anyone else on the coaching staff, but got the word from tight end Pat Freiermuth after it was announced on Tuesday night. Rodgers said that the change came after "months of conversation" about the offensive operation, including the playcalling, and that "things went to a different place" in recent days.

Rodgers said that McCarthy fell asleep in an quarterback meeting last Wednesday and missed other meetings leading into their loss to the Eagles on Sunday. Rodgers said McCarthy also broke down the team with "1-2-3 Packers" at halftime of that game and that McCarthy was not regularly watching film while preparing for games. Rodgers said he also believes McCarthy has lost the team in general.

"Everybody in that building knows the truth," Rodgers said.

Rodgers said similar things happened when the two men were with the Packers and that he believes McCarthy blames him for being fired in Green Bay after the 2018 season. He said he saw that McCarthy was not connecting with Steelers players early in training camp, but tried to help smooth things out.

"I protected him," Rodgers said. "I didn't talk about the things publicly. I didn't talk about his habits."

Rodgers also said he pushed to have changes made to the playcalling and game-planning that he believed were going to take place before Tuesday's benching pushed things in a different direction. Rodgers said that he told the team that if they weren't going to make those alterations that they should release him and said that there was no chance of a reconciliation with the team after how they handled things on Tuesday.

"That ship has sailed," Rodgers said.

The comments guarantee that Steelers players will be asked for their accounts of how things have been in the building since McCarthy's arrival this offseason and their responses will likely determine whether or not things go completely off the rails for the team in the final weeks of the season.

item.title: Why the first matchup between the 49ers and Seahawks was so strange
item.description: Don’t expect the same chaos on Sunday
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers defeated the Seattle Seahawks in Week 5, 32-29. To say it was a strange game is an understatement. It was also thrilling and exhilarating. Wins are wins in the NFL, but this win was particularly odd given how it played out. The 49ers’ defensive line was excellent. The secondary was exceptional. The offense converted in the red zone, as they have done so effectively this season.

So, what made this game so odd? Despite the score, this was the highest-scoring defensive struggle I may have ever seen. How can you call it a defensive struggle with over 60 total points? Let me explain. The 49ers scored a touchdown on a George Holani fumble before halftime. The Seahawks scored points on the back of a Jacob Cowing muffed punt.

Deebo Samuel popped his hamstring and fell flat on his face, and the ball came loose for another turnover on the plus side of the field for Seattle. In fact, the initial touchdown for the 49ers started with a Renardo Green interception deep in Seattle’s territory. Now, the reason I point this out is that turnovers were the story of this game.

Seattle’s offense likely doesn’t score much without turnovers. The 49ers certainly capitalized on their turnovers, and the biggest drive of the game was a drive that started from the Seattle 26 in the fourth quarter, which was punctuated by a seven-yard touchdown catch by Brandin Cooks.

The reason I point all these things out is that it’s hard to expect this type of scenario and, at times, sloppiness from both teams again. Turnovers will be a major part of the story on Sunday as Sam Darnold returns, and if he continues the trend of turning the football over, it will hinder Seattle’s chances.

With Darnold as the quarterback, the only stretch of football he has played without turning the football over was from Week 18 (against SF) through the playoffs with a Super Bowl win. That’s a four-game stretch. I’m willing to bet he’s going to make some mistakes on Sunday. Seattle’s defense is still elite, in a much different way than Minnesota is, but if turnovers happen and Seattle is backed up defending their own end zone, that’s a recipe for success for the 49ers.

Week 5 was filled with chaos and jaw-dropping scenarios. I expect Sunday to be far more composed and just as tight a matchup.

item.title: Tackling will be of utmost importance for Bills vs. Chiefs offense
item.description: The specific reason why tackling will be vital for Bills vs. Chiefs
item.content:encoded:
What do I think the biggest — and specific — defensive key for the Buffalo Bills against the Chiefs on Thanksgiving night?

I’ll provide some metrics, and you’ll be able to reach the answer.

The Chiefs are:

  • First in screen-pass rate in the NFL entering this game at 16.4%,
  • Third in RPO rate at 8.4%

and Patrick Mahomes has the:

  • Third-lowest average depth of target (aDOT) at 6.6 yards among 38 qualifiers
  • Fourth-quickest average time to attempt at 2.51 seconds among those same qualifiers
  • Fourth-lowest percentage of throws made 20-plus yards downfield at 9.2% among 33 qualifiers
  • Second-highest adjusted completion percentage at 81.1%

You guessed it — tackling.

The Chiefs, more than any other offense, put their opponent’s tackling capabilities to the test.

How well have the Bills tackled this season, you ask?

Below is a graphic that demonstrates the total amount of missed tackles credited to Bills defenders in each game by Pro Football Focus to date this season:

After the bye week, which coincides with when CJ Gardner-Johnson was no longer on the team, the Bills have averaged six missed tackles per contest.

In the six contests before the bye, Buffalo was averaging 8.5 missed tackles per game.

Remember, before the spitting incident in Las Vegas, Gardner-Johnson was the owner of the highest missed tackle rate among qualifying safeties in the NFL.

And don’t forget, on August 11, Bills defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard said the following during a press conference on this very topic:

“Who can finish, get guys on the ground? That was an Achilles’ heel here last year. So that’s the No. 1 thing we have to correct.”

Per PFF, in the regular season, the Bills averaged 8.88 missed tackles per game during the 2025 campaign. In Buffalo’s two playoff outings last season, that figure jumped to 9.5 per.

Right now, even with the noticeably bad start, Buffalo’s missed tackles per game average is down to 7.5.

And another strong showing in the tackling department for the Bills will go a long way in securing a win over the Chiefs on Thanksgiving night.

item.title: Caleb Williams Week 11 QB Grade: Bears vs Saints Film Breakdown
item.description: A deeper look with @iamcogs at Caleb Williams and the Chicago Bears’ 21-13 win over the Saints!
item.content:encoded:
A Quick Note: Due to holiday travel plans I won’t be doing in-depth breakdown with individual plays, we will return to those for Week 12!

Coming off the bye, I think many of us expected a little more fireworks from the Bears offense against New Orleans. Instead, Chicago started slowly, put together consecutive touchdown drives to open up a 16-0 lead, and largely managed the game from there in a 21-13 win. It wasn’t particularly pretty, but the Bears improved to 8-2 with their fifth straight victory.

Caleb Williams capitalized on both of the defense’s second-quarter takeaways, finding D’Andre Swift on a 3-yard shovel pass before connecting with Colston Loveland for a 15-yard touchdown. Loveland supplied the highlight with a hurdle over Julian Blackmon, while Williams helped turn those extra possessions into some breathing room.

Williams finished 15 of 23 for 181 yards, two touchdowns and one interception on a deflected pass. There were opportunities left on the field, but I think the context of what he was being asked to do matters quite a bit this week.

My charting had Williams attempting a pass from under center on just four of 28 dropbacks, a 14.3% rate compared with his season mark of 32.8%. That’s an 18.5-percentage-point drop, and a noticeable departure from Chicago’s usual approach.

The formation and personnel numbers added another layer. Chicago used at least three receivers aligned wide on 15 of those 28 dropbacks, while 19 came in 11 personnel. That 67.9% dropback rate stands out alongside the Bears’ 49.4% overall season usage, although those aren’t identical samples. I don’t have a seasonal baseline for the wide alignments, so that number is descriptive rather than proof of an increase.

Fellow WCG writer Lester Wiltfong Jr. came away with a similar impression of the simplified game plan. With Detroit waiting on Thanksgiving, it wouldn’t surprise me if Johnson kept some things close to the chest. That’s my read, though, rather than something these numbers can establish.

StartKyleOrton pointed out that Chicago ran the ball 20 times on first down, with just four classified as successful. That’s useful context when evaluating Williams, because an ineffective running game can make the passing game’s job considerably harder. I can see the argument that Johnson wanted to work through some of those issues, but whatever his intent, the offense’s overall production and Caleb’s individual performance deserve separate consideration.

None of that gives the offense a free pass. New Orleans cut the lead to 16-10 before halftime, and Chicago needed a third-quarter field goal to restore a two-possession cushion. Still, with the defense producing six sacks and Montez Sweat adding a fourth-quarter safety, Williams didn’t have to carry this one.

It was a workmanlike win with plenty to clean up before Thursday. With the short turnaround, let’s get right into the benchmarks.

Benchmarks

(Season totals are underlined, Season Averages in Italics, and this week’s stats appear in regular text.)

C/A:134/195 (68.7%) | 22.3/32.5 (68.7%) | 15/23 (65.2%)

Yards:1546 | 256 | 181

Touchdowns:10 | 1.7 | 2

Turnovers: 5| 0.8 | 1

QB at Fault Sacks:1 |0.2| 2

aDOT: 7.7 | 10.9

Passer Rating: 95.4 | 100.1

True Passer Rating:115.7 | 139.7

Time to Throw:3.10s | 2.84s

Time to Pressure:2.55s | 2.55s

Pressure Rate:37.05% | 34.482%

On-Target Rate:85.9% | 68.4%

Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 5.6% PPR / 8.8% BRP | 0.0% PPR / 12.9% BRP

EPA per dropback:+0.15 | -0.01

ANY/A: 6.6 | 6.4

Game Scorecard

The full grading sheet for each play can be found here.

Game Notes

NFL Passer Rating / True Passer Rating / PFN Impact Score: 100.1 / 139.7 / 76.7

  • The NFL’s average passer rating through Week 11 sits at 91.3, putting Williams’ 100.1 comfortably above that mark and 11th among qualifying quarterbacks this week. His two touchdown passes helped offset the interception, producing a respectable result despite the offense’s uneven afternoon. His ability to remain efficient with a 7.9 yards per attempt also helped keep his passer rating healthy.
    • This is where the box score and the individual grading can tell slightly different stories. Williams finished with a good passer rating, but that doesn’t mean his accuracy or execution was consistently where we’d like it to be (or where we’ve seen it for the most part of the year.)
  • A 139.7 TPR represents a “Great” outing, matching the mark Williams posted against Seattle in Week 8.
    • That result adds some perspective to an uneven afternoon. His accuracy wasn’t as consistent as we’d like, particularly underneath, but the quality of his better plays still deserves recognition, hitting on 5 of his 7 throws beyond 10 yards and posting a season high 10.9 aDOT also helps.
  • On the PFN scale, where 75 represents an average qualifying starter and 90 is elite territory, Williams finished Week 11 with a 76.7 Impact Score, ranking 10th among 26 qualifying quarterbacks.
    • That’s a slightly above-average result and a reasonable reflection of the afternoon overall. Williams contributed to the win, but this wasn’t a performance that required him to carry the offense or consistently overcome difficult circumstances.

On-Target Throws: 2026 Average: 85.9% | Week 11: 68.4%

  • Reminder: Completion percentage ≠ On-Target Percentage. I only chart aimed passes, meaning throwaways, spikes and passes deflected at the line are excluded. Drops can still be credited as on-target.
  • Short-Level Passing (Behind LOS–9 yards): 8/12 | 66.7% On-Target
  • Deep-Level Passing (10+ Yards Downfield): 5/7 | 71.4% On-Target
    • This was the most disappointing part of Williams’ afternoon for me. He finished on target on just 13 of 19 aimed throws, putting him 17.5 percentage points below his season mark.
      • And while the misses we’re say at the level we saw in early 2025, it was an uncharacteristic outing in the context of 2026.
    • The short-level accuracy stands out in particular. Four off-target throws on 12 attempts underneath is a considerable amount of missed execution in an area where we’ve seen greater consistency in 2026.
      • Worth noting, 2 of those 4 off-target throws were still caught, they just required beyond ordinary effort relative to the throw difficulty.
    • Williams was actually more accurate on throws traveling at least 10 yards downfield, although seven attempts is a small sample. The takeaway isn’t that the deeper passing was flawless, but that the shorter throws weren’t providing the dependable efficiency this offense needed.

Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 0.0% PPR / 12.9% BPR

  • Williams finished without a “Poor” graded play while still producing a 12.9% Big Play Rate. That combination helps explain how he earned a “Good” final grade despite the accuracy issues.
    • An off-target throw doesn’t automatically qualify as a “Poor” play in my grading. Accuracy, decision-making, difficulty and the circumstances of the play all matter, so the lower on-target percentage and clean Poor Play Rate aren’t contradictory.
    • His interception goes “Ungraded” because it came on a pass deflected at the line of scrimmage. Under my grading approach, I don’t assign quarterback blame for the unpredictable outcome of those deflections, and in most cases a defensive lineman leaving his feet is the fault of the offensive line.
      • That doesn’t erase the turnover or its impact on the game. It means I’m separating the result of the play from what I’m assigning to Williams individually.

EPA per Dropback: 2026 Average: +0.15 | Week 11: -0.01

  • Williams finished just below neutral at -0.01 EPA per dropback, a noticeable step down from his +0.15 season average. There were productive moments, but the passing game didn’t generate sustained efficiency across the afternoon.
    • Conversely, EPA isn’t as forgiving as my individual play grading. The interception carried a -3.25 EPA value, regardless of the deflection or whether I assigned Williams blame.
    • That’s a useful example of why I include multiple measures. EPA captures the damage the turnover did to Chicago’s scoring outlook, while the film grade evaluates Williams’ responsibility for the play. Both provide context, but they’re answering different questions.

ANY/A: 2026 Average: 6.6 | Week 11: 6.4

  • Williams’ 6.4 ANY/A landed slightly below his season average of 6.6. The two touchdowns helped support that figure, while the interception and two sacks pulled it back down.
    • Much like passer rating, ANY/A charges Williams for the interception regardless of how it happened. Even with that penalty, he finished close to his season baseline.
    • The league average mark currently sits at 6.1, so Williams is still outperforming the average quarterback in the NFL.

Time to Throw: 2026 Average: 3.10s | Week 11: 2.84s

  • Williams averaged 2.84 seconds to throw, finishing 0.26 seconds below his season average. The ball was coming out faster than usual, which fits the broader picture of a different offensive approach against New Orleans, especially the decrease in under center and play-action throwing.
    • Paired with the short-level accuracy numbers, this is an area I’d like to see sharpened against Detroit. Williams doesn’t need to hold the ball longer to improve the results. More consistent execution on the available throws would be a good place to start.

Summary

Williams finishes Week 11 with grades of 1st Half (2.50) / 2nd Half (0.95) and an adjusted final Game grade of 4.20, with the adjustment applied because he fell below the 39-play threshold. That gives him a “Good” graded game, his fifth in seven outings this season.

It wasn’t his most impressive performance, and the quieter second half reflects that. Still, Williams helped turn two defensive takeaways into touchdowns, made enough plays to get Chicago across the finish line, and avoided anything resembling the turnover-filled outing we saw against Tampa Bay.

All that said, there are some trends to keep an eye on in the coming weeks. Interior pressure has increased, contributing to the majority of Williams’ turnovers and sacks over the last few games. I also saw a few reps where his footwork looked reminiscent of 2025 Caleb Williams, with inconsistent mechanics and some old habits creeping back in.

There were even moments where it almost seemed like he was battling his old self midgame. His 40-yard completion to Zavion Thomas was the most notable example. His feet started to get choppy, but he caught himself, settled and fired a dot downfield. The result was great, but the process is still something worth monitoring.

I’ll be watching how Ben Johnson and the Bears’ offensive line address the interior pressure, along with whether Williams can clean up his footwork and hit his checkdowns more consistently. One of his sacks came after he passed up an available checkdown to try to extend the play. Those are opportunities to keep the offense moving that I’d like to see him get back to taking more often.

But it really helps when the Bears can win without asking their quarterback to do everything, or be perfect. Thanks in part to great coaching led by Ben Johnson, who picked up his 20th win as Chicago’s head coach, moving to 20-9 including the playoffs. For some perspective on how different this has felt, the Bears already have two five-game winning streaks under Johnson, compared with one across the previous 12 seasons combined. We can pick apart an uneven offensive performance while still appreciating how much the expectations around this team have changed.

Then there’s Jeffery Simmons, who apparently decided two sacks in his first two Bears games weren’t enough. His three-sack afternoon against New Orleans brought him to five in three games with Chicago. As John Todd noted during the game, Simmons became the first Bear since Khalil Mack in 2018 to reach at least four sacks in his first three appearances with the franchise.

The broader defensive numbers from SumerSports are just as encouraging. Since Simmons arrived in Week 8, Chicago’s blitz rate has dropped from 39.6% to 22.0%, while its pressure rate has barely moved, going from 40.9% to 40.2%. EPA allowed per dropback has improved from -0.03 to -0.27. Simmons doesn’t get sole credit for that entire shift, but being able to generate pressure while keeping more defenders in coverage gives Dennis Allen considerably more flexibility.

Now comes Detroit on Thanksgiving, with very little turnaround time. I’d like to see Chicago create more favorable passing situations and Williams deliver a more complete performance across both halves. The Bears took care of business against New Orleans, but Thursday is an opportunity to pair that winning result with sharper execution against a division rival.

Until next time, Bear Down!

Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs.

item.title: Aaron Rodgers goes scorched earth on Mike McCarthy after Steelers benching: Live updates
item.description: Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers spoke on The Pat McAfee Show about his benching and said he will not return to play for Pittsburgh.
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Rodgers appeared on the Pat McAfee Show on Wednesday, Nov. 25 to address his benching by the Pittsburgh Steelers for their NFL Week 12 matchup with the Denver Broncos on Black Friday.

The team announced late Tuesday night that Mason Rudolph would start the game and that Rodgers would be inactive following a pair of losses against the Cincinnati Bengals and Philadelphia Eagles that have dropped Pittsburgh to seventh in the AFC standings.

"This has been months of conversation leading up to the last couple of days when things went to a different place," Rodgers said, who claimed tight end Pat Freiermuth told him the news of his benching. He said he still hasn't talked with general manager Omar Khan about the decision.

He explained that the word "benching" never came up with coach Mike McCarthy, but that communication with him had been strained. Rodgers said that McCarthy had been "snoring" in team meetings or had missed them entirely over the past week.

At halftime of the loss to the Eagles on Nov. 22, Rodgers claimed that McCarthy led a cheer for the start of second half by referring to the Packers, his former team. Rodgers then questioned whether McCarthy was healthy, seeming to question his awareness going back to training camp at Saint Vincent College in Latrobe.

Rodgers confirmed meetings took place into Tuesday and felt that he was addressing his thoughts about McCarthy on behalf of the team. He said that McCarthy denied the behaviors that Rodgers observed, but that multiple other players in the locker room would vouch for having witnessed them. Later, he was explicit in saying that he didn't wish for McCarthy to be calling the plays.

Aaron Rodgers says Mike McCarthy's behavior is 'disrespectful to the game'

"I don't think he knows the plan," Rodgers said. "I think he learns the plan during the week. ... That part is disrespectful to the game itself."

Rodgers then connected the problems in Pittsburgh to the end of McCarthy's tenures in Green Bay and Dallas before saying he asked McCarthy for his release if the coach acted to bench him.

Rodgers called it "comedy" that general manager Omar Khan would defend McCarthy's behavior while knowing about it. And he argued that the changes should have happened earlier while contrasting McCarthy's process with that of other coaches, including Green Bay's Matt LaFleur and Los Angeles' Sean McVay.

McAfee replied that he was worried about McCarthy after hearing what Rodgers said.

Later, Rodgers contrasted McCarthy's style with that of former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin. He argued that many players -- including some of the biggest veteran stars -- did not know McCarthy very well personally, which was a departure from how Tomlin handled things.

He said the problems began almost immediately after his return to the Steelers in May and that any players so situated like him with "nothing to lose" would say as much, too. He bemoaned that too many people inside the facility were dependent upon McCarthy and the team to speak up.

Will Aaron Rodgers return to Steelers?

As for his future, Rodgers indicated that he is done with the team and won't be moving forward with it in what he's said will be his final season.

"At this point, I'm not going back to Pittsburgh," Rodgers said. "That ship has definitely sailed."

He ripped the front office, including principal owner Art Rooney II, for not acting on the word of the players about the problems with McCarthy that he had observed.

Rodgers regretted that the behaviors were not different from earlier in McCarthy's career, given McCarthy's ties as a Pittsburgh native. He called it "insanity" that things weren't different and lamented that he wouldn't get to move forward with teammates whom he respected and he insisted "felt the exact same way."

Steelers offense struggled before Aaron Rodgers benching

The struggles of the Steelers offense in recent weeks have been profound. Rodgers did not complete a pass for most of the first half Nov. 15 against Cincinnati. The game had been decided for all practical purposes by the time he threw his pair of touchdown passes for the night.

A week later against the Eagles, the Steelers scored just three first-half points. Rodgers was sacked five times and struggled to get a rhythm going with top receiver DK Metcalf, who was ejected after a pair of unsportsmanlike conduct penalties. He caught one pass for two yards and has just 60 yards over the past three games. The vast majority of them came in garbage time against the Bengals.

Injuries have played a part in the ugly run. No. 2 receiver Michael Pittman Jr. has been out since Week 4. He's dealt with foot injuries since training camp.

The absence of left guard Mason McCormick, meanwhile, has caused the running game led by Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle to stall. Warren has just 43 total rushing yards in the past two games, which has put pressure on Rodgers and the passing game to compensate.

Aaron Rodgers planned final season with Steelers

Rodgers signed a one-year deal to return to the Steelers in May and cited the relationship with McCarthy from their days in Green Bay as an enticing reason to return for his 22nd season. McCarthy was his coach for the Packers' Super Bowl victory at the end of the 2010 season and two of his four MVP award wins.

However, Rodgers also indicated upon returning that this season would be his last in the NFL.

With that definitive ending in place, the Steelers made the unorthodox decision to keep four quarterbacks on their 53-man roster coming out of training camp. Rodgers and Rudolph were joined by second-year signal caller Will Howard, a former sixth-round draft pick, and rookie Drew Allar, whom general manager Omar Khan selected out of Penn State in the third round of the April draft in Pittsburgh.

Those two will now serve as Rudolph's backups and could push for playing time if he struggles as the team looks toward a possible future with one or both.

Rodgers has apparently taken an active role in their development, passing out assignments to keep them busy during the week when they're not getting practice reps.

“I really appreciate it because I’ve heard from other guys around the league that it’s not like that in every room,” Allar told the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette last week. “He’s kind of the rare exception.”

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Aaron Rodgers goes scorched earth on Mike McCarthy after Steelers benching: Live updates

item.title: Insider sees a troubling path to Puka Nacua’s next Rams deal
item.description: Puka Nacua might have played his final game in a Los Angeles Rams uniform. He also might not have. ESPN NFL insider Adam Schefter weighed in on Nacua’s future during...
item.content:encoded:
Puka Nacua might have played his final game in a Los Angeles Rams uniform. He also might not have.

ESPN NFL insider Adam Schefter weighed in on Nacua’s future during Tuesday’s episode of “The Adam Schefter Podcast.”

“Here’s what I would say: He’s an unrestricted free agent! And he’s an unrestricted free agent coming off a knee injury. I think they want to keep him. I think they plan to keep him. Will they actually keep him? We’ll see,” Schefter said.

“The offseason, there’s a lot of things that come up. Puka obviously is serving a suspension now, he had off-the-field issues last offseason, now he’s got a knee injury that was operated on,” Schefter added.

“He’s coming off the knee, he’s a free agent, there has been a suspension; the Rams would like him back. He’s gonna want to get paid… so how is this all gonna work out? I think it’s a mistake to say he’s not back in LA, and I think it’s a mistake to say it’s automatically [back]. We don’t know!”

Schefter believes the Rams plan to keep Nacua. Whether the two sides can agree on a price remains an open question.

Losing Nacua would leave a sizable hole in the Rams’ passing game. He’s developed into one of the NFL’s best receivers in Los Angeles.

Los Angeles still has a season it needs to focus on, including a critical game against the Green Bay Packers on Wednesday night.

But Nacua’s contract situation will become the biggest story to follow for the Rams once their 2026-27 campaign concludes.

item.title: NY Giants’ Abdul Carter named the NFC Defensive Player Of the Week
item.description: NY Giants pass rusher Abdul Carter has been recognized for his dominant game against the Jaguars
item.content:encoded:
New York Giants edge defender Abdul Carter has been named the NFC Defensive Player Of the Week for his incredible performance against the Jacksonville Jaguars.

Carter had an absolutely dominant game against the Jaguars, notching 12 quarterback pressures, 6 of which were quick pressures, 2.0 sacks, 5 QB hits, 4 tackles, and 2 tackles for a loss. He was the only player across the NFC with multiple sacks and five quarterback hits in Week 11.

Carter is beginning to truly break out and is becoming the player the Giants envisioned when they took him 3rd overall out of Penn State.

Carter told doubters to stand back and watch his game against the Jaguars prior to Week 11. He said that he’d have a big game, then backed it up by terrorizing Trevor Lawrence.

“He’s been saying the same thing to me,” coach John Harbaugh said after the game. “But more than that, he’s been practicing that way. So to see him break out and get the sack and the quarterback hits, it was great.”

“Twelve pressures, did he? Twelve pressures,” Harbaugh added. “Should have given him two game balls, I guess.”

Carter said after the game that he and the rest of the defense answered the call to shut down a good Jaguars team.

“These are the games that all of our best players got to play their best,” said Carter. “We’ve got a team like that. You are what your record says you are. They’ve got a great record, they’ve got a great team. We proved we’re that, too.”

Carter, 23, has already become one of the most feared and disruptive pass rushers in the NFL despite this beeing just his third season at outside linebacker. Per NFL NextGenStats, this was just the fourth time this season a player put up those types of numbers without an unblocked pressure.

So far this year, Carter ranks:

  • 1st in the NFL in Time To Pressure (2.17 secondsj)
  • 2nd in Pass Rush Win Rate (28 percent)
  • 1st in Quick Pressure rate (76 percent)

After the game, RT Jermaine Eluemunor credited Carter’s elite get-off for his disruptiveness and compared him to truly elite company.

“There’s a lot of guys in the NFL that are really talented but don’t have that get-off,” Eluemunor said “Just anticipating the snap count, but then also being able to have that get-off. Because there are a lot of guys that jump the snap count, but they don’t have that first explosive step that he has. That explosive step that he has is really rare in this league. Only a couple of guys have it. Micah Parsons has it, Myles [Garrett] has it, Will Anderson has it, and those are three of the best in the NFL. He can anticipate the snap count, but then he also has that explosiveness to help with that.”

“[Abdul] thinks he’s the best and he’s going to start playing like that,” Eluemunor added. “He’s been playing like that, but I think that in this game, you truly got to see the hard work and the film study that he’s been putting in and just the emphasis he’s put on just trying to be that player. I think that’s the first of many games he’s probably going to have like that this season.”

It’s also an increasingly common occurrence to see a Giant be recognized for their play. All told, this is the 6th time this year that a Giant has earned Player Of The Week or Month honors.

  • S Jevon Holland was the NFC Defensive Player Of The Month for September.

item.title: Matthew Stafford has to play well against the Green Bay blitz
item.description: The Rams need to counter the Packers’ pressure
item.content:encoded:
Quarterback Matthew Stafford has to beat the blitz if the Los Angeles Rams want to defeat the Green Bay Packers Wednesday night. If he can’t, L.A. is in big trouble.

Considering how important this game is for the Rams’ playoff chances, there’s no alternative for finding a way to counter one of the Packers’ best weapons.

Green Bay has done a good job getting after the quarterback this year. It’s second in the NFL in pressure rate at 40.2% according to Next Gen Stats, only behind the 46.2% clip of the Minnesota Vikings.

While the Packers don’t blitz nearly as much as Brian Flores and the Vikings do, their defensive coordinator, Jonathan Gannon, still brings plenty of extra pass rushers. Green Bay has the NFL’s eighth-highest blitz rate at 35.8%.

Meanwhile, this has not been Stafford’s best season against blitzes. For the year, he’s 18th in the NFL in EPA per dropback when blitzed, actually giving away .06 points per dropback in those situations. Considering he has the sixth-most pass attempts when blitz, that’s a lot of ineffective plays over the balance of the season.

For comparison’s sake, when not blitzed this year Stafford is ninth in the league in EPA per dropback.

The Packers like to blitz. Stafford has struggled against the blitz. You can see where this is headed on Wednesday night.

The Rams can find a few ways to mitigate this issue. For one, Stafford is throwing short (0-9 yards) on 49.5% of his dropbacks this season. The Packers have been good at limiting yards after the catch this season, but getting the ball out quickly can help neutralize the extra pressure.

Obviously, the offensive line has to play well. That shouldn’t be particularly concerning for the Rams, because they’ve handled pass protection well all season.

Los Angeles is ninth in ESPN’s Pass Rush Win Rate metric and they’re seventh in the NFL in PFF’s pass protection grades.

There’s also one other potentially interesting wrinkle involved here: Micah Parsons.

The three-time first-team All-Pro will make his season debut Wednesday after missing the Packers’ first 10 games due to recovery from a torn ACL. It goes without saying that the Rams would prefer to not face one of the best pass rushers in the league, one of the few other players even in Myles Garrett’s stratosphere.

But we also don’t know what the Packers will look like defensively with him on the field. Gannon said earlier this month that he has game planned for Parsons’s return “every day,” but he’s never actually coached him before. Will the Packers continue to blitz at a well above-average rate with him back? Or will they try to win with just four and bank on Parsons adding enough juice to make up for it?

The Packers want to attack you and they will want to attack the Rams. They have an interception-hungry secondary and want to use their blitz pressures to force quarterbacks into bad throws.

If Matthew Stafford can avoid that quagmire, either thanks to his offensive line or his own heroics, the Rams’ offense should be in good shape. If it remains an issue, there will be far more pressure on the Los Angeles defense to carry this game.

item.title: Where the Seahawks’ elite defense has fallen off from 2025
item.description: The Seahawks defense is terrific, but there are some areas where they’ve dropped in performance from last year.
item.content:encoded:
If you look at some of the major stats for the Seattle Seahawks defense, they’re roughly averaging the same points allowed as last season’s Super Bowl team, they’re once again ranked No. 1 overall by DVOA, No. 1 in EPA/play, No. 1 in fewest pass yards allowed, and tied for first with the San Francisco 49ers in fewest yards allowed per carry.

And yet, there are times where the Seahawks do not feel like their defense is as great as 2025. We’ve got a few stats to show where things have noticeably dipped.

Red zone defense

Thanks to the Carolina Panthers, the Seahawks are no longer the worst red zone defense by EPA/play. Holding the Arizona Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders to just a touchdown on four red zone trips means Seattle has improved it’s red zone TD percentage to 29th, but this is still a perplexingly bad RZ defense until further notice.

Last season, the Seahawks were fifth in red zone TD percentage defensively and No. 1 in red zone DVOA. Generally speaking, red zone numbers are smaller sample size and such a huge disparity between Seattle’s RZ and non-RZ defense should signify future positive regression. The Seahawks defense has been put in many unenviable spots due to short-field turnovers, but it wasn’t like short-field turnovers weren’t happening last year. Something is not clicking in the micro structure of Seattle’s red zone defense.

4th down defense

Almost the same deal as red zone defense. Seattle was 10th-best at stopping 4th down in 2025, but this year the ‘Hawks have sunk to 31st. Last year’s 4th down defense ranked 2nd in EPA/play, while the 2026 unit is 31st overall and 32nd against the run. Their only two stops on 14 attempts came in garbage time against the Kansas City Chiefs and the goal line stand late in the second Cardinals game.

While the Seahawks boast a fantastic 3rd down defense, we live in an era where going for it on 4th down more often is strongly encouraged, and the Seahawks have struggled to slam the door shut on all four downs. Again, small sample size that can normalize as the season progresses, but much like the red zone, it’s not necessarily guaranteed.

It’s certainly notable that in both the red zone and 4th down, Seattle’s otherwise airtight run defense is at or near the bottom in EPA, so something is not clicking in the trenches the way it did last year.

Defending No. 1 receivers

FTN’s DVOA metric has long included metrics for opposing defenses against receivers, running backs, and tight ends. The Seahawks 2025 pass defense was not only the best in the NFL overall, they were the best at defending No. 1 wide receivers. Admittedly, the designation of a No. 1 receiver is “somewhat subjective” by DVOA criteria, but most teams have a clear top wide receiver target.

Anyway, the 2026 Seahawks is once again tops by pass defense DVOA, but defending top receivers is a big dropoff to 22nd. The DVOA breakdown includes WR1, WR2, WR3, TE, and RB, and WR1 is the only one for which Seattle is outside the top 10.

Seattle’s schedule of opposing offenses is an impressive 8th, with only the Denver Broncos, Arizona Cardinals, and Los Angeles Chargers ranked in the bottom-half in pass offense DVOA. However, when the Seahawks have been tasked with facing what I would assume are top receivers, the results haven’t been overly impressive:

Mike Evans had 7 catches for 113 yards and a touchdown in the first 49ers meeting, while Terry McLaurin caught 6 passes (all but one of which went for a first or a touchdown) for 77 yards and a touchdown in the Commanders game. The Bears’ WR1 is presumably Luther Burden, who was shut out in the second half against Seattle but had 7 catches for 56 yards and a score. All but one of Burden’s catches would be classified as a successful play based on yardage gained relative to down and distance. Seattle didn’t have to play Rashee Rice at all, Ladd McConkey checked out early with an injury (and the Chargers offense reeks anyway), and A.J. Brown had 3 catches for 26 yards and a DPI penalty drawn before he left in the second half with his own injury.

For the next three weeks, the Seahawks will face Evans again, CeeDee Lamb, and Malik Nabers, so the schedule of wide receiver opposition will not let up in the short term.

Make no mistake about it, though: The Seahawks defense is still great and they’re not close to the main reason the team is currently sitting outside of a playoff spot. Seattle’s offense needs to improve significantly to have any shot at contention, but the defense also needs to fix its micro problems that have factored into close games swinging against them.

item.title: Brandon Aiyuk reportedly signs with Washington Commanders practice squad as free agent, reuniting with former college quarterback Jayden Daniels
item.description: Aiyuk is looking to play in his first NFL game since 2024.
item.content:encoded:
Veteran wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk has signed with the Washington Commanders practice squad as a free agent, ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported on Wednesday.

Free-agent WR Brandon Aiyuk is signing with the Washington Commanders practice squad, per his agent Drew Rosenhaus. Aiyuk once again becomes teammates with his Commanders QB Jayden Daniels. pic.twitter.com/jt8diY95o3

— Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) November 25, 2026

Aiyuk was released by the 49ers on Monday and passed through waivers on Tuesday, going unclaimed. Now, he reunites with his former teammate at Arizona State, quarterback Jayden Daniels.

The Commanders, fresh off a stunning upset over the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 11, have been in need of help at receiver following a season-ending injury to star wideout Terry McLaurin. The team sits at 4-5-1, just two games back from the New York Giants, who hold the lead in the NFC East.

This marks a fresh start for the 28-year-old, who signed a four-year, $120 million contract extension with the 49ers ahead of the 2024 season but played just seven games on the new deal. He tore his ACL and MCL on Oct. 20, 2024, ending his season.

Aiyuk also missed the entirety of the 2025 season, with conflicting reports about his health as he rehabbed the knee injury. The distance between the two sides only grew as San Francisco voided his contract guarantees ahead of the 2025 season. Eventually, he was placed on the Reserve/Left Squad list in December 2025 due to his continued absence and lack of communication with the team.

This past January, 49ers GM John Lynch officially acknowledged the impending split, saying at his end-of-season news conference, "I think it's safe to say he's played his last snap with the 49ers."

Aiyuk was officially reinstated from the Reserve/Left Squad list on Nov. 9, at which time the 49ers were granted a two-week roster exemption to decide if they wanted to release him, trade him or add him to the 53-man roster. The reinstatement was the first step toward Aiyuk's eventual release.

San Francisco drafted him with the 25th pick in the 2020 NFL Draft. He had his breakout season in 2022, finishing with 1,015 yards and eight touchdowns. Aiyuk returned in 2023 and improved, finishing with 1,342 yards and seven touchdowns.

item.title: Commanders sign Brandon Aiyuk to practice squad after 49ers release
item.description: After an acrimonious split with the 49ers, Brandon Aiyuk landed with the Washington Commanders. Here's how he fits with former teammate Jayden Daniels.
item.content:encoded:
Brandon Aiyuk has found a new NFL home after his acrimonious split with the San Francisco 49ers.

Aiyuk is signing with the Washington Commanders' practice squad, his agent Drew Rosenhaus told ESPN. The veteran visited with the team on Wednesday, Nov. 25, and a deal quickly came together.

Aiyuk spent the first six years of his career with the 49ers but did not play during the 2025 season while recovering from a torn ACL and MCL suffered midway through the 2024 campaign.

San Francisco coach Kyle Shanahan and general manager John Lynch both acknowledged something went awry with the relationship between the player and team during the season. However, neither detailed exactly what happened.

"I say it officially stopped for me when last time I tried to get ahold of him and couldn't," Shanahan said regarding the communication between Aiyuk and the franchise. "Then tried a couple more times and still couldn't, and then that matched everyone else that was trying to get ahold of him and couldn't. Eventually there's not much of an explanation, because it's really hard for us and anyone else to understand."

The 49ers voided all guarantees in Aiyuk's contract in November after the receiver "failed to attend meetings and declined to participate in other team activities," according to The Athletic.

Aiyuk told the NFL Players Association he wouldn't file a grievance to contest the move, and he was placed on the reserve/left squad list in December.

That same month, Aiyuk posted a video of himself to his YouTube account that showed him speeding past the Levi's Stadium – home of the 49ers – in Santa Clara. Aiyuk was traveling at speeds exceeding 90 mph while exceeding 100 mph on the freeway once. The speed limit in the area where Aiyuk was driving is 25 mph.

The drama between Aiyuk and the 49ers bled into the 2026 NFL offseason and regular season. Aiyuk posted numerous videos during the offseason calling the organization "stupid" and "dumb" in one video while asking for his release. He also posting several photos and videos of him wearing a Commanders hat while airing his grievances.

More: Brandon Aiyuk's Instagram timeline, from 49ers rants to Jayden Daniels jabs

Eventually, Aiyuk hired well-known agent Drew Rosenhaus and applied for reinstatement, Two weeks after being reinstated, the 49ers released Aiyuk, subjecting him to waivers, which he cleared, before becoming a free agent who was able to sign with any team.

The Commanders ended up signing Aiyuk despite what Shanahan referred to as a "confusing" end to Aiyuk's time in San Francisco.

The Commanders' general manager, Adam Peters, spent seven seasons as part of the 49ers front office and was the team's vice president of player personnel when it selected Aiyuk in the first round of the 2020 NFL Draft. Aiyuk also played one season alongside Jayden Daniels at Arizona State, giving him built-in chemistry with the star quarterback.

Here's what to know about Aiyuk's deal with the Commanders and how he will fit in Washington.

Brandon Aiyuk stats

Aiyuk didn't play in 2025, but he posted back-to-back 1,000-yard seasons in 2022 and 2023 while being named an All-Pro second teamer in the latter. Below is a full look at his stats across the 69 games he played for the 49ers.

  • Targets: 446
  • Receptions: 294
  • Receiving yards: 4,305
  • Receiving TDs: 25
  • Yards per reception: 14.6
  • Carries: 13
  • Rushing yards: 117
  • Rushing TDs: 2

How does Brandon Aiyuk fit with the Commanders?

Aiyuk will add some much-needed depth and upside to the Commanders' receiving corps. Washington lost its No. 1 receiver, Terry McLaurin, to a torn patellar tendon, and his future with the team is in question because of the injury.

Beyond McLaurin, the Commanders has Stefon Diggs on its roster, but the 11-season veteran is only on a one-year deal with the franchise. Elsewhere, rookie fourth-round pick Antonio Williams has flashed at times, most notably in his nine-catch, 122-yard outing against the Cincinnati Bengals on "Monday Night Football" in Week 11, but Washington will need more than just him to surround Daniels with quality pass-catching weapons long-term.

While Aiyuk's time with the 49ers ended on a sour note, he was reliable force across his first four NFL seasons. He missed just six total games over that span while averaging 74 catches, 1,078 yards and seven touchdowns per 17 games played.

Aiyuk is entering his age-28 season, so time remains for him to bounce back from injury and round into a quality starting receiver again. And Aiyuk's preexisting relationship with Daniels from their 2019 season together at Arizona State should only improve his potential for clicking in Washington.

Either way, the Commanders are risking very little by bringing the 2023 All-Pro second-teamer in to see exactly what he has in the tank.

item.title: Brandon Aiyuk joins the Commanders’ practice squad
item.description: A couple of 49ers are poised to reunite in Washington
item.content:encoded:
The least surprising transaction to happen on Tuesday was former San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk visiting the Washington Commanders. While Aiyuk has yet to sign officially, it was a move that was the most predictable outcome.

The Commanders need a wideout. Former 49ers general manager Adam Peters now runs the show in Washington. Aiyuk’s college quarterback, Jayden Daniels, just so happens to be under center in DC.

During a radio appearance on Wednesday, Peters called Aiyuk one of the “hardest workers on the team” when he was with the 49ers. “One of the things that I don’t think anyone can dispute is his work ethic. That’s how he became an All-Pro-type player. He was a true No. 1 receiver at the time. He’s a guy who’s a tough cover; he’s great after the catch. There’s a lot of great things about him on the field. It wasn’t just that he was the most gifted guy; he’s self-made too. There’s a lot of positives.”

The caveat “on the field” is doing a lot of work here. While the 49ers may have had some buyer’s remorse after his injury, Aiyuk put on a clinic of what not to do for the past year and a half. That’s why he was released.

Peters, who hasn’t spoken to Aiyuk in “a couple years,” continued. “I can’t speak on all what happened between him and the 49ers. What I do remember is he’s a very motivated player.”

Maybe there was no resolution to be had. But you’d think if Aiyuk had any kind of motivation left, he would’ve swallowed his pride and gone to work for the team with the best record in the conference. Doesn’t winning on the big stage have to mean something?

Again, there was likely no coming back from whatever the “situation” was, but Aiyuk had every reason to be motivated last year, when we saw him running routes in August in a preseason game with the team. Then, as the year went along, a No. 1 receiver never emerged. Aiyuk could’ve been the top target for a playoff team.

The motivation is different now. It’s been two years since Aiyuk played in the NFL. Unless he’s training against NFL defensive backs on the side, he hasn’t gone against the best competition in the world since a season-ending knee injury. Expecting anything close to the 1,300-yard receiver feels like a long shot.

We’ll keep a close eye on whether Aiyuk signs to Washington’s practice squad and where the two sides go from there, but this story is far from over.

Kyle’s update, 10:00 am PT: ESPN’s Adam Schefter tweeted that Aiyuk finished up his visit with the Commanders, but there won’t be a deal today. Here’s Schefter’s quote from Drew Rosenhaus: “Discussions are ongoing and positive. Probably no decision today.”

Aka, we could not agree on terms today.

Kyle’s update, 10:20 am PT: So much for that. About twenty minutes later, Aiyuk is joining the Commanders’ practice squad.
