item.description: Malik Mustapha no longer has a strike on his record this season
item.content:encoded:
Over a month ago, when the San Francisco 49ers were in Seattle, the NFL fined safety Malik Mustapha for a “hit on a defenseless player.” It was on the final drive of the game that Mustapha hit Jaxon-Smith Njigba.

Raheem Morris calls it the “strike zone,” which is above the belt and below the neck. That’s where Mustapha hit JSN, yet the NFL still felt the need to step in.

The league fined Mustapha $6,998. Mustapha will be happy to get those funds back. More importantly, from the 49ers’ perspective, it means Mustapha no longer has one strike to his name. This year, three violations of specific offenses equal a one-game suspension.

Mustapha came close against the Cowboys. The kind of force Mustapha plays with, he’ll always come close to what’s deemed “unnecessary” in today’s NFL. So, getting one strike back could pay dividends in the second half of the season.

Back in Week 5, Mustapha had another collision where he de-cleated Rashid Shaheed. It was clean and in the strike zone, but a lot of these flags, and eventually penalties, stem from the result or how a player peels himself off the turf. There were a couple of those in Week 5.

Malik should not change who he is. He made a difference the last time these two teams met. Hopefully, he won’t be fined for tackling again.

item.title: Chiefs-Bills Week 12 Final injury report: Kenneth Walker ruled out
item.description: The final injury news for the Week 12 game between Kansas City and Buffalo.
item.content:encoded:
Each practice day this season, the Kansas City Chiefs release an official injury report ahead of the next game. In Week 12, the Chiefs play the Buffalo Bills on Thanksgiving night.

Here is the Chiefs’ final official injury report of the week, courtesy of the team’s official website.

After Monday’s practice estimates, Tuesday’s report showed the teams on the field preparing for the game.

Chiefs

  • Running back Kenneth Walker (groin) was ruled out after being upgraded to a limited participant and practiced Tuesday for the first time since injuring his groin before the Week 10 game against the Atlanta Falcons.
  • Starting right tackle Jaylon Moore (ankle) was ruled out after he did not participate in practice again and hasn’t since leaving the Week 9 game against the New York Jets in the third quarter with an ankle injury.
  • Second-year defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott (knee) was ruled out after he was a limited participant in practice all week for the third consecutive week. He was activated from the Reserve/Physically-Unable-to-Perform list last week.
  • Tight end Noah Gray (rib) is questionable after he was upgraded to a full participant in practice after missing on Monday after leaving the game against the Arizona Cardinals late with the injury.
  • Right guard Trey Smith (concussion) has no game designation after he was a full participant in practice again; he appears set to return after entering concussion protocol during the first quarter of the Week 10 game.
  • Rookie defensive tackle Peter Woods (neck) is questionable to play for the first time since leaving the game injured against the Denver Broncos in Week 8.

Bills

The following information is from Tuesday’s injury report. Check back in for Buffalo’s final injury designations.

Starting cornerback Christian Benford (groin) was upgraded to a limited participant after he was estimated to not participate in practice on Monday and missed last week’s game. In eight games played this season, Benford has 33 tackles and eight passes defended. In his career against Kansas City, Benford has 2 passes defended, one sack and a forced fumble.

Starting right tackle Spencer Brown (back) was upgraded to a full participant in practice after being estimated as limited on Monday. He missed time earlier this year, but has played in the last two games.

Starting tight end Dalton Kincaid (thumb/ankle) was a limited participant in practice on Tuesday after being estimated as limited on Monday. He missed last week’s game and has been banged up for a few weeks. This season, Kincaid has seen the second-most catches on the team (32) and has 487 yards and two touchdowns; Kincaid has one touchdown in his career against the Chiefs.

Starting right guard O’Cyrus Torrence (ankle) has been a limited participant in practice this week; he has not missed a start this year.

Starting linebacker Dorian Williams (calf) has been a limited participant in practice this week after missing last week’s game. This season, Williams has 61 tackles (5 for loss), one sack, two interceptions and four passes defended.

item.title: What the numbers say about Cowboys vs Eagles
item.description: How can the Cowboys take care of business on Thanksgiving?
item.content:encoded:
Every week, we’ll examine the numbers behind the next opponent on the schedule. Looking at the recent numbers and trends for each team, we’ll add it all up to see which squad may have the edge. This week, the 5-6 Dallas Cowboys look to get back to .500 against the 3-7 Joe Milton-led Philadelphia Eagles.

Cowboys key stats from last week

Dak Prescott continued his recent hot streak, completing 28/33 passes for 325 yards and four touchdowns. He’d also cash in with his legs, scoring once on the ground. Prescott currently ranks second in the NFL in pass yards and passing touchdowns, just behind Joe Burrow in both categories. Over the last two weeks, the Cowboys quarterback has put up ten touchdowns, 668 passing yards, and a passer rating of 123.5.

CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens each crossed the century mark on the day, recording 132 and 102 yards respectively. Each finished with a touchdown against the Titans.

Quinnen Williams and James Houston each recorded two sacks and had a combined five tackles for loss. The defense played their best game of the season against a Titans team that came in averaging 27 points per week over the last three games.

Eagles key stats from last week

The Eagles snapped a seven-game losing streak with former Cowboys quarterback Joe Milton leading the team. Milton finished the day 11/21 for 141 yards and a 73.7 passer rating. He did not score.

Saquon Barkley scored the only Eagles touchdown on the day. He totaled 17 carries for 75 yards against the Steelers.

Philadelphia’s biggest weapon was the right leg of Jake Elliot who went 4/4, the longest coming from 55 yards out.

The defense recorded five sacks and held the Steelers to just 255 total yards and 16 points.

Stack up points early

We’ve seen Joe Milton’s cannon arm here in Dallas. The power he possesses is truly amazing. And while his accuracy has improved since last year, he still is not a starting-caliber NFL quarterback at this point in his career. He’ll overthrow balls at times and his decision making isn’t the best.

The Cowboys can take advantage of Milton’s vulnerabilities by playing complementary football for the second straight week. Dallas held the Titans to just three field goals in the first half last week while putting up four touchdowns of their own. If the offense and defense are synced up like that again on Thanksgiving, this could be another big game for this team.

If Dallas allows Saquon Barkley to get going and doesn’t force Milton into mistakes while simultaneously struggling on offense, you’ll see a close game that goes down to the wire. While Dallas may not be a good team, the Eagles are exponentially worse. Force them to play keep up with a Cowboys offense that’s firing on all cylinders and this will be a fun Thanksgiving day for the Dallas players and fans alike.

What do the numbers mean?

Containing a banged up Saquon Barkley will be the biggest key for Dallas in this game. If the defense forces Joe Milton to win through the air, the Cowboys win this game by multiple scores. If Barkley consistently gives the Eagles third and short while keeping the offense on track, Dallas will have a game on their hands. They simply cannot allow that to happen.

Brian Schottenheimer needs to ride the hot hand and allow Dak Prescott and his receivers to cook while also utilizing the running game in a complementary capacity. The offensive line has been hot as well, playing their best game of the year last week against the Titans. Play the game with points on the brain and forget about time of possession. This week, quick scoring drives benefits the Cowboys more than long, methodical drives. The Eagles will try and shorten the game while Dallas needs to focus on quick strikes and explosives to run up the score.

Notably, the offensive motion rate has dramatically increased over the past few weeks. This should continue again this week, helping Prescott diagnose the defense pre-snap and creating mismatch opportunities. Watch for big plays from the Cowboys receivers this week with Quinyon Mitchell likely out and Tariq Woolen filling in. We’ve seen Lamb beat Woolen earlier this season, so finding that matchup will be key again this time around.

Last week was the first time we saw it all come together for Dallas, blowing out a team they were meant to walk over. Take care of business early and we’ll see opportunities for turnovers from Joe Milton pressing to play keep up in a game where Dallas is likely put up another huge point total. If all goes to plan, the Cowboys should win this game handily on Thanksgiving.

item.title: Bills Week 11 game balls: Greg Rousseau and James Cook reach career milestones
item.description: Handing out game balls from Week 11
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills took care of business against the Miami Dolphins in Week 11, securing a 26-9 divisional victory at Highmark Stadium before turning their attention to a Thanksgiving night matchup with the Kansas City Chiefs.

Buffalo out gained Miami 405-185, controlled the football for 36:45 and held the Dolphins to just two third down conversions on 14 attempts. Perhaps most impressive was the defense’s ability to keep Miami out of the end zone for all four quarters.

There was plenty to celebrate in Buffalo’s locker room following Sunday’s victory, including a new career high for one defensive standout and another historic accomplishment for the Bills’ running back.

Let’s take a look at who received game balls from head coach Joe Brady before handing out a few of our own.

EDGE Greg Rousseau

“Look, I could give this to everyone on defense the way y’all are playing right now,” Brady said before awarding his first game ball to Greg Rousseau.

And rightfully so. Buffalo’s defense held Miami to just 185 total yards, 10 first downs and three field goals.

But Rousseau finished the afternoon with three solo tackles, two sacks, two tackles for loss and two quarterback hits, accounting for both of Buffalo’s sacks and costing the Dolphins a combined 16 yards.

His first sack came on Miami’s opening offensive possession when he brought down quarterback Kyle McCord for an eight yard loss on third and six, forcing the Dolphins to punt.

With his two sack performance, Rousseau reached 10 sacks on the season, establishing a new career high with six regular season games still to play.

Perhaps equally impressive is that Rousseau accomplished all of this while playing just 34 defensive snaps.

RB James Cook

Brady’s second game ball went to James Cook, who continues to rewrite the NFL record books.

Cook finished Sunday’s contest with 22 carries for 89 yards and a touchdown.

According to Brady, Cook became the first player in NFL history to record at least 75 rushing yards and a touchdown in nine consecutive games. Brady also recognized Cook for reaching 1,000 rushing yards for the fourth consecutive season. And there’s still plenty of football left to be played.

What continues to impress me about Cook is his consistency. Even on an afternoon when Buffalo averaged just 3.5 yards per rushing attempt as a team, Cook found a way to produce and extend his historic streak.

Sara’s Game Ball: WR Khalil Shakir and WR DJ Moore

I’m going to cheat a little bit this week and award my game ball to two players because, quite frankly, I couldn’t justify recognizing one without the other.

Khalil Shakir and DJ Moore combined for 13 receptions on 19 targets for 192 receiving yards and a touchdown, accounting for nearly 63% of quarterback Josh Allen’s 304 passing yards.

Shakir hauled in five of nine targets for a team leading 101 receiving yards, averaging an impressive 20.2 yards per reception. Moore, meanwhile, led Buffalo in both receptions (eight) and targets (10), finishing with 91 receiving yards and a touchdown.

What stood out most to me about Moore’s performance was his production on third down. Converting on three third downs.

While Shakir provided the explosive plays, Moore consistently helped keep the chains moving. Their complementary performances were instrumental in Buffalo’s ability to sustain drives and dominate the time of possession.

Both deserve recognition this week.

Honorable mentions

K Tyler Bass

When your kicker accounts for more than half of your team’s points, he certainly deserves some recognition.

Bass connected on four of five field goal attempts and both extra point attempts, accounting for 14 of Buffalo’s 26 points.

While Buffalo’s inability to consistently finish drives in the end zone remains an area of concern, Bass made sure those possessions didn’t go to waste.

P Tommy Doman

Imagine making the honorable mentions list as a punter without recording a single punt.

Facing fourth and eight from Buffalo’s own 34 yard line in the first quarter, the Bills dialed up a fake punt. Doman connected with tight end Keleki Latu for a 30 yard completion.

You can say it… the entire call was borderline disrespectful and I loved every minute of it.

RB Ty Johnson

While Cook continues to make headlines with his historic rushing performances, Ty Johnson deserves recognition for his contributions to Buffalo’s passing attack.

Johnson hauled in seven of eight targets for 55 receiving yards. He finished second on the team in receptions despite playing just 28 offensive snaps.

Johnson was particularly effective in helping Buffalo sustain drives. His versatility continues to be a valuable asset to Buffalo’s offense, and Sunday’s performance was another reminder of just how important his role can be.

On the the next

There’s little time to celebrate, however, with Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs coming to town on Thanksgiving night.

Who gets your game balls this week, Bills Mafia?

item.title: Puka Nacua’s MCL ‘completely’ tore off the bone as gruesome injury details emerge
item.description: Further details of the knee injury that ended Puka Nacua's season early are emerging — and they're gruesome.
item.content:encoded:
Further details of the knee injury that ended Puka Nacua’s season early are emerging — and they’re gruesome.

ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported on Tuesday that the Rams wide receiver tore his MCL “completely” off his shin bone when he was hit in the fourth quarter of Los Angeles’ Nov. 8 win over the Commanders.

Additionally, Schefter said Nacua “had a tear off the posterior oblique portion of the MCL as well.”

“So that wouldn’t have healed with the stability that they needed and essentially, it would be performance-limiting with a higher chance of earlier degenerative changes,” Schefter said on “The Adam Schefter Podcast.” “So they had to go in and repair the knee.”

Nacua went under the knife on Nov. 17 to fix the issues, and he’s since been given a 4-to-5-month recovery timeline.

The 25-year-old has somehow appeared to remain in good spirits despite the situation, as he shared a couple positive updates on his Instagram page on Tuesday.

In the first, he showed a picture of him on a trainer’s table with a breakfast burrito and the caption, “Recovery.” In the second, he shared a snap of him with his son with the same caption.

Schefter, though, wondered if the injury — coupled with all of his offseason drama, his recent NFL suspension and his status as an impending free agent — could signal the end of his time as a Ram.

“I think they want to keep him,” Schefter said of Nacua’s potential future in Los Angeles. “I think they plan to keep him. Will they actually keep him? We’ll see.”

The NFL insider later added, “There’s a lot of questions that are going to sort themselves out this offseason with Puka Nacua.”

item.title: NFL Thanksgiving preview: Bills and Chiefs renew a fun rivalry with big stakes in AFC playoff picture
item.description: The Bills are leading the AFC with a 9-1 record, and the Chiefs are a game behind.
item.content:encoded:
No matter who else is in the AFC playoff picture, the Buffalo Bills will always have an eye out for the Kansas City Chiefs.

Since Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen entered the NFL, the Chiefs and Bills have met four times in the playoffs. Allen and the Bills have lost all four times. Allen hasn't made a Super Bowl yet despite having a great career, and the biggest reason is Kansas City has stood in the way.

The Chiefs had a stunning 6-11 record last season but have bounced right back. They're 8-2 to start this season. But the Bills are 9-1, and can practically knock one team out of its way in the race for the No. 1 seed by beating the Chiefs on Thursday.

The big question for the Chiefs was if Kenneth Walker III could return from a groin injury, abut the Chiefs ruled him out on Wednesday. Rookie Emmett Johnson has played very well in his place, but Walker was one of the best backs in the NFL for the first half of the season. The Chiefs could miss him in a huge game.

Johnson playing well is important because there could be bad weather. The forecast is for about 37 degrees with a 75% chance of rain at kickoff. There's also expected to be 19 mph winds, which could affect passing games.

The Bills will be looking to ride Josh Allen for a big home win. With Allen, the Bills are 0-4 against the Chiefs in the playoffs, but 5-1 in the regular season against Kansas City. Another regular-season win over the Chiefs wouldn't ensure that they could knock off Kansas City in the postseason, if the two teams meet again, but it would likely mean that matchup would be in Buffalo.

Who needs it more?

The Bills aren't getting endless shots at making a Super Bowl with Josh Allen. At some point this era will end, and it would be tremendously disappointing if it didn't include at least one trip to the final game. It's hard to think that far ahead, but this game is huge for the Bills in not only getting closer to the AFC's No. 1 seed but also making sure they won't be going to Kansas City in January. The Broncos, Jaguars and Bengals are all in the mix for the No. 1 seed, too, but the Chiefs have been such a problem for the Bills in the playoffs that it's OK to have a little more focus on being in a best position just in case they meet Kansas City again. The Chiefs don't want to fall two games behind the Bills and also lose ground on the Broncos in the AFC West, but this is a bigger game for Buffalo.

Key player: Chiefs WR Josh Downs

Downs has played just 28 snaps for the Chiefs since they acquired him in a trade with the Colts. But in those 28 snaps he has 10 targets, which is a great sign that Patrick Mahomes already trusts him and wants to get him involved. Downs has eight catches for 112 yards and a touchdown with Kansas City, which is tremendous efficiency for playing less than 25% of the offensive snaps in two games. The big question for this game will be if Downs is comfortable enough in the offense to take on at least half of the snaps in a huge game. Downs has already shown he can impact the Chiefs' offense, even without playing much. His role on Thursday will be a big story.

Betting market watch

Vikings-49ers was billed as the Game of the Year last Sunday; hopefully, Chiefs-Bills lives up to the hype. Buffalo has been good to bettors overall (8-2 against the spread) and at home (4-1 ATS), while Kansas City has lost both games outright and ATS on the road against potential playoff teams this season (20-3 at Seattle, 28-24 at Denver). Patrick Mahomes has also thrown for 942 yards and 10 TDs (with no INTs) in Kansas City's last three blowout wins against less competition (NY Jets, at Atlanta, Arizona). Buffalo has won six straight — including the last four by at least 17 points — but still seems a little under-discussed for a 9-1 football team. Mahomes is an impressive 13-4-1 ATS as an underdog in his career. My gut says Josh Allen finds a way to get this done. He saves his best for Mahomes, Andy Reid & Co. — and this is the regular season, where Allen has dominated this matchup. The Bills (-3) cover another classic between these two great QBs. — Ben Fawkes

Check out more of Ben's work at the Yahoo Sports betting hub.

Fantasy football storylines

We're getting one of the NFL's best games of the year when the Chiefs travel to Buffalo on Thanksgiving night, though an ominous weather forecast (cold, rainy, windy) could affect the results. Here are three fantasy themes to track as you finish up the Thanksgiving slate.

1. Can Emmett Johnson do it again? The Chiefs wanted to get Kenneth Walker (groin) back after a two-game absence, but Emmett Johnson has been undeniably great as the temporary fill-in. Over the last two games he has 206 rushing yards and 108 receiving yards. He’s in for another big workload on Thursday.

2. How much will Josh Allen run? Although Allen has continued to pile up the short-yardage touchdowns, his rushing production has been muted this year — he has just 51 rushing yards in the last five games, and he didn't have a single rushing attempt against Miami last week. The Chiefs have seen Allen plenty over the years, so they know how important it is to limit this element of his game.

3. What's the featured pitch in the Chiefs' passing game? Travis Kelce is coming off a two-score week, Josh Downs has hit the ground running with his new team, and Rashee Rice is a consistent factor on shorter routes. Patrick Mahomes is spreading the ball around, so it's hard to view any of these guys as an automatic fantasy start. But there's a plausible upside for all three, as well. — Scott Pianowski

The Panthers have opened the practice window for linebacker Thomas Incoom.

Incoom has been designated for return from injured reserve and will be able to practice for the next 21 days as a result. The Panthers can activate him at any point in that window.

Incoom was placed on injured reserve ahead of Week 7 due to a calf injury. He had six tackles and a fumble recovery in five games before his injury.

The Panthers have now designated seven players for return this season. They will be able to do it one more time during the regular season and that spot is expected to be filled by cornerback Jaycee Horn once he is ready to get back on the field.

item.title: For the first time in years, it’s fun to watch the Commanders play defense - Daily Slop
item.description: Led by rookie standout Sonny Styles, Frankie Luvu, Nick Cross, K’Lavon Chaisson, and a top-11 run defense, Daronte Jones has given Washington an identity it has lacked for years
item.content:encoded:
The Daily Slop – 25 November

Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

Commanders links

Articles

Bullock’s Film Room (subscription)

Commanders Film Review: Defense vs Bengals

This was a new Cover-0 look that I don’t recall seeing from Jones so far this season. Traditional Cover-0 is pure man-to-man coverage against all eligible receivers and no safety help in the middle, but this is almost like a three-deep zone variation of Cover-0. The Commanders put eight defenders on the line of scrimmage this time and all eight of them blitz. That leaves just three defenders in coverage as they effectively play the deep zones of Cover-3 behind the blitz.

Burrow again looks to his top receiver in Ja’Marr Chase, but this time Chase is in the slot and spotting up as a hot route option. Burrow immediately pulls the trigger to avoid a sack and throws hot to Chase, but cornerback Rasul Douglas plays this perfectly. Douglas sits at the first down marker knowing the ball has to come out quick against the blitz. He knows Chase is Burrow’s go-to target and he spots Chase beginning to slow down and spot up underneath. So before Burrow even delivers the throw, Douglas begins breaking on the pass. This enables Douglas to arrive at Chase before the ball does and he goes over the top of him to nearly intercept the pass.

Unfortunately, Douglas drops the interception on what would have been an outstanding play by him. It goes back to what I said on the previous play, the Commanders biggest issue defensively is finishing plays when they have the opportunity. Douglas dropped three interceptions in this game and this was one of them. It was still a terrific read and great play by Douglas, but it could have been so much better had he come up with the ball.

It’s a fun variation of Cover-0 because it’s not really Cover-0 when you have three zone defenders deep, but it also is Cover-0 because the Commanders only have three defenders in coverage. The Bengals had four receivers running routes so the Commanders were outnumbered in coverage, but that’s the risk you sometimes take to commit to the blitz and force a hurried throw underneath that can lead to interception opportunities.

Jones stayed aggressive throughout the game, dialing up various blitzes that were all fairly effective. But it was Cover-0 that he came back to in the most critical moment.

The Athletic (paywall)

The Commanders defense was like a new language; they’re getting more fluent

This mini-Commanders renaissance — three wins in four games, consecutive victories for the first time in 22 months — is due in no small part to a defense that was tasked with learning a new language in the offseason, and is only now able to think in that language without clumsily running it through a translator in their brains. The pauses are fewer. The flow is better. The results are coming.

Witness: This is a defense that just held Joe Burrow and the absolutely steamrolling Cincinnati Bengals to an output below their season averages across the board.

Early in the season, when Washington started 1-3-1, the Commanders allowed chunk plays in bunches —ranking 16th in the percentage of plays that went for at least 20 yards — and couldn’t sustain efforts through the second half. In this quasi-revival — a 3-2 stretch that includes an understandable, competitive loss at San Francisco — they have tackled better, gotten more consistent pressure on the quarterback and limited gash plays.

What’s happening is clear. First-year coordinator Daronte Jones arrived in Washington from Minnesota — and you should check out the body of work by his old Vikings boss Brian Flores — with the task of building a new, more aggressive system from the ground up. The build takes time. But it’s happening.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

From Commanders Roundtable:

Cincinnati entered Monday night converting an NFL second-best 51.9% on third down, yet Washington held them to just 4-of-12 (33.3%) on the night. Against an offense averaging 29.8 points per game, keeping the Bengals off the scoreboard for the first 21 minutes was a clear statement. Aside from two isolated explosive plays—a 44-yard catch-and-run by Samaje Perine late in the second quarter and a 31-yard touchdown strike to Higgins right before halftime—the Commanders kept a tight lid on every big-play threat Cincinnati threw at them.

What looked like an outlier a month ago is rapidly becoming Washington’s identity. The Commanders have now held four consecutive opponents to 21 points or fewer—and they haven’t padded those numbers against bottom-feeders. That stretch includes offensive heavyweights in San Francisco, a healthy Los Angeles Rams squad, and now Cincinnati.

Against a Cardinals offense ranked 29th in scoring (17.3 points per game), 25th in total yards, and carrying a steep -132 point differential, Jones’ group has a golden chance to keep rolling.

To read more of this Commanders Roundtable article, CLICK HERE

Athlon Sports

How Did Jayden Daniels Do in Week 11 vs. Bengals?

Jayden Daniels spent most of Monday’s first half dodging Boye Mafe in the rain at Northwest Stadium, and the Washington Commanders went into the locker room trailing a Cincinnati Bengals team that had won five straight.

By the end of the night, he had thrown for 289 yards, run for 55 more and needed only two throws to Antonio Williams to set up Drew Stevens’ winning kick in a 22-20 win.

So how did he do? Slow start, strong finish. Daniels went 23 of 35 with no touchdown passes and no interceptions, a 91.2 passer rating and a 58.6 QBR, per ESPN’s box score. Those numbers undersell the second half, when Washington scored on six straight possessions for the first time in 48 years, according to ESPN’s John Keim.

ESPN

Commanders coach Dan Quinn fine with Stefon Diggs’ sideline rant

During a first half in which Washington struggled to move the ball, Diggs appeared to be frustrated after a third down sack in Bengals territory. He was open on a crosser on third-and-4, but Daniels did not throw the ball, instead trying to escape the pocket to his left. But Boye Mafe sacked him from behind.

That led to Diggs yelling, appearing to direct his anger at Daniels to “throw the f—ing ball’ or at the offensive line that “he can’t throw the f—ing ball.”

“I love his fire, I do,” Quinn said. “I love that. There’s a lot of good that comes with it where it can sound like he’s mad but it’s like some energy that comes behind it.”

Indeed. Though it took two more series, the Commanders did finally find some offensive energy. They scored on their last possession of the first half — the first of six consecutive scoring drives.

Before Diggs’ sideline rant, Daniels had completed 4 of 5 passes for 25 yards but was sacked twice and scrambled once.

Starting on the last drive of the first half, Daniels completed 19 of 24 passes for 264 yards. Whether or not that stemmed from Diggs’ fire is uncertain — Daniels wasn’t asked about it postgame.

Sports Illustrated

Commanders Get Brandon Aiyuk’s First Visit. Monday Night Changed What Awaits Him

Where Would He Fit in Washington?

Monday night made that question more interesting. Antonio Williams caught nine passes for 122 yards against the Bengals, including gains of 22 and 42 yards on the final drive that set up rookie kicker Drew Stevens’ winning field goal. Stefon Diggs caught four passes for 45 yards, and Treylon Burks caught two for 30. Williams played 57 of Washington’s 68 offensive snaps Monday. With McLaurin out, the Commanders have reason to examine another receiver, but Williams has already earned a substantial role. Aiyuk’s 2023 resume alone shouldn’t put him ahead of Williams, who has earned the snaps he’s getting.

NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport has suggested a practice-squad start, which would let Washington bring Aiyuk into the offense without immediately opening a spot on the 53-man roster. That remains a possibility, not an agreement. It also would not put a date on his first game.

It is not obvious how quickly Aiyuk, 28, could contribute to a new team, since he hasn’t played a game in more than two years. Aiyuk has two more years remaining on his contract with salaries of approximately $27.3 million and $29.2 million, and if a team had claimed him, it would have acquired both him and his contract.

If Aiyuk signs to the Commanders’ practice squad, he could earn a maximum salary of $22,850 per week.

Also from The Athletic:

“One of the things that I don’t think anybody can dispute is his work ethic,” Peters said Wednesday during his paid weekly appearance with the Sports Junkies on 106.7 The Fan. “He’s one of the hardest workers on the team, and that’s how he became an All-Pro type of player for us in San Francisco — (it) was his work ethic and his drive to get better. And so the last season I was there, he had a fantastic season. … He was a true No. 1 receiver at the time.”

But Peters reminded that there’s a difference between being in shape and in “football shape.”

“There’s context to everything, and Brandon hasn’t played in over two years, and he’s coming off a major knee injury,” he said. “ … As much as you can do those things, you can’t replicate what you do out on the football field, in an NFL practice or in an NFL game. So those are the things we’re going to look at and see where he’s at. I think we’d all be foolish to say that he’s going to jump right on to where he left off. But that’s what we’re going to look at, and our expectations are gonna be accordingly.”

Peters told the Junkies that he “can’t speak to the last couple years” with Aiyuk because he hasn’t spoken with him directly in that time.

“I’m really looking forward to seeing him today and catching up with him,” Peters added. “So I can’t speak on all that or what happened between him and the 49ers. But what I do remember of him is kind of what I said to you guys earlier. He’s a very motivated, self-motivated player who’s an extremely hard worker, and he’s a smart football player.

“And those are the things that led him to get that contract that he got because he earned all that by doing all those things and doing the right things in and out of the building when I was there. So, looking forward to talking to him today and kind of just checking in on him and seeing how he’s doing, how his family’s doing and all that.”

The Marvin Harrison Jr. experience crashed and burned in the biggest of ways this season with Arizona trading the No. 4 overall pick and a 2027 seventh-rounder to the Houston Texans for a second-round pick and 2027 sixth-rounder.

item.description: All games picked for one of the most compelling weeks of the season.
item.content:encoded:
It was inevitable.

After flirting a couple of times with landing under .500 in a given week of picks, it finally happened. For Week 11, I went 6-7.

That's what I get for trying to pick upsets. In Week 11, it was Chalk City — and 12 of 13 home teams won.

And so, from now on, I'm not getting cute. I'm sticking with my first impulse. I'm not overthinking it. The first number that pops into my head will be the pick.

For the year, I'm at 102-60-1. The success rate is still 62.5 percent. Here's hoping I can find a way to push it a little higher with the 16 games to be played from Wednesday through Monday.

Packers at Rams (Wednesday night)

Sean McVay is 0-5 against Matt LaFleur. A loss on Wednesday night would put the preseason favorites in grave danger of missing the playoffs, especially in light of an upcoming schedule that includes games against the Chiefs, the 49ers, the Cowboys, the Seahawks (twice), and the Buccaneers.

Rams 24, Packers 20.

Bears at Lions (Thursday)

It's the biggest early-window Thanksgiving game ever, with both teams at 8-2. Ben Johnson's Bears gave up 52 points during last year's visit to Ford Field. They'll be determined to achieve a different result this time, in what becomes a true litmus test for the new-look Bears. If they're truly contenders, this is a game they win.

Bears 23, Lions 21.

Eagles at Cowboys (Thursday)

It won't be a cakewalk. For Philly, it's the closest they'll get this year to a game with a postseason vibe. But the Cowboys have a chance to make a run at the Giants — if Dallas can also hold off the Commanders.

Cowboys 41, Eagles 24.

Chiefs at Bills (Thursday)

Josh Allen is 5-0 against Patrick Mahomes in the regular season, 0-4 against Mahomes in the postseason. The trend continues, thanks to conditions that are more conducive to Allen making the right throw at the right time.

Bills 23, Chiefs 17.

Broncos at Steelers (Friday)

This one had the feel of a game the Steelers would find a way to win, until the benching of Aaron Rodgers threw everything into disarray.

Broncos 20, Steelers 13.

Saints at Bengals

The Bengals need to get back on track, quickly, after Monday night's sluggish performance. A slump could open the door for the Browns to steal the division.

Bengals 31, Saints 20.

Ravens at Texans

It feels like an elimination game in Houston, even if the winner will still be facing an uphill climb to the postseason. When in doubt, ride with the clearly better quarterback.

Texans 27, Ravens 23.

Giants at Colts

This will be a far cry from the 1958 NFL Championship. The Giants are surging, and the Colts are slowly disintegrating.

Giants 24, Colts 9.

Titans at Jaguars

As the saying goes, it's not the size of the dog in the fight but the size of the fight in the dog. Unfortunately, this fight is round two of Doberman vs. Chihuahua.

Jaguars 35, Titans 20.

Jets at Dolphins

The Dolphins are running out of chances to get a second win (if they even want one).

Dolphins 23, Jets 13.

Falcons at Vikings

Kirk Cousins gets the double whammy — his first home game in his second stint with the Vikings, and his first shot at revenge against the team that signed him and then drafted his replacement.

Vikings 27, Falcons 13.

Patriots at Chargers

It's fitting that a game pitting two struggling teams coached by former Ohio State and Michigan players happens one day after a game between struggling Ohio State and Michigan teams.

Patriots 16, Chargers 10.

Commanders at Cardinals

Monday night's upset of the Bengals means nothing if the Commanders bungle a winnable game at Arizona.

Commanders 27, Cardinals 10.

Seahawks at 49ers

Having an extra week to prepare, coupled with the urgency of a 6-4 record, is just what the doctor ordered for the Seahawks.

Seahawks 27, 49ers 23.

Raiders at Browns

The NFL will be happy it flexed this one into primetime. (For reasons other than getting Patriots-Chargers out of that window.)

Browns 30, Raiders 27.

Panthers at Buccaneers

Tampa Bay is running out of chances to pull themselves back into contention.

Buccaneers 27, Panthers 20.

item.title: Eagles vs. Cowboys Game Preview: 5 questions and answers with the Thanksgiving enemy
item.description: ﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿Opponent insight on Philadelphia’s upcoming matchup.
item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Eagles can avoid being some real turkeys by beating the Dallas Cowboys on Thanksgiving. Fans would be very thankful to see a Birds win on Thursday.

In order to preview this Week 12 NFC East battle, I reached out to our enemies over at Blogging The Boys. The divine Dave Halprin kindly took the time to answer my questions about this upcoming battle. Let’s take a look at the answers.

1 – To what extent do you buy Mike Pettine taking over play-calling making a positive difference for the Cowboys’ defense? 

I’d say it somewhat made a positive impact. The defense against the Titans on Sunday certainly looked more coherent, especially in their coverage and with players being in proper position. There didn’t seem to be so many busted assignments and guys not knowing what to do at the snap. 

There are reports they simplified the defensive calls and ran more zone coverage on the back end. The Titans did score three touchdowns, but one came on a questionable pass interference call in the endzone, another on a fluky run-after-catch where the Cowboys defender thought he touched the guy down but didn’t, then a garbage time TD at the end of the game. So the 30 total points kind of seems larger than how it felt in the run of the game. Of course, having an offense score 51 points overwhelms all issues, but it still felt like a little bit better version of the Cowboys defense. 

2 – Besides Christian Parker being demoted, what else has significantly changed for the Cowboys since they last played the Eagles?

For one, the pass rush, While the Cowboys overall defense still struggles, in the four games since we last played the Eagles, Dallas has accumulated 17 sacks with plenty of other pressure that forces bad plays. Quinnen Williams has really taken his game up a notch and is terrorizing teams from the middle of the line. The defense still struggles against the run, and besides Joey Porter Jr. our cornerbacks can definitely be had on a regular basis. But the pass rush has become the one thing that really works on defense.

On offense, it feels like Brian Schottneheimr has re-discovered motion, play-action, bunch sets, cutdown splits and other things that were severely under-used in the earlier part of the season. The Cowboys scored 40 points on a very good 49ers defense, and 51 points over the hapless Titans defense. The last two games have been more reminiscent of how good the offense had been previously rather than the inconsistent bunch we’ve seen at times in 2026. 

3 – If the Cowboys lose to Joe Milton at home on Thanksgiving, would that be their most embarrassing possible loss this season? What’s the path to the Cowboys losing this game? 

While it would be a bitter pill to swallow, we’ve already hit new lows by losing at home to a then-winless Buccaneers squad playing without Baker Mayfield, and allowed the terrible Cardinals to put together a comeback for the ages to win in Dallas. So losing to Joe Milton would make every fan gnash their teeth and then scream about not keeping him, but beating those other losses in the embarrassment category would be a hard thing to do. But, I won’t count the Cowboys out, they just might find a way to out-embarrass themselves.

The path to losing the game is kind of the same every week. The Cowboys defense plays horrible football, busting assignments, gathering penalties and basically making a joke out of form tackling. Then the offense goes into one of its inconsistent modes, where the play-calling is bad and penalties, drops or turnovers come home to roost. 

4 – Which NFC East team is going to win this division? Who’s going to finish second, third, and fourth? 

I was really leaning to the Cowboys because I just kept believing that the Giants would start to fall apart with their backup QBs playing. But that Jacksonville game where the Giants held on to victory makes me think that decent coaching (John Harbaugh) really can turn a team around. I’m still holding out hope we can catch them, but if I had to lay my life savings down on it, I’d have to take the Giants. As for the rest, it will probably end up the way it is now – Cowboys second, Commanders third and Eagles fourth. 

5 – Who wins this game and why? With the Cowboys currently listed as 8.5-point home favorites, what’s your score prediction?

I’m taking the Cowboys because they are at home where the offense usually plays well, and the defense looks like it might just be getting incrementally better. The Eagles are trying to overcome a lot this season including injuries at QB and at other key positions. There just feels like  a lot of turmoil over there and the Cowboys might be in the process of starting to play like we expected them to when the season began. I’ll take the Cowboys 31-23.

item.title: Fantasy Football Week 12 Panic Meter: Emeka Egbuka isn't in a slump anymore — this is who he is
item.description: The Chiefs backfield, Trey McBride, Colts offense and more from Ray Garvin in the Week 12 fantasy football panic meter.
item.content:encoded:
We're past the point in the fantasy football season where we can afford to be patient. It's playoff crunch time, and for a lot of fantasy managers, every lineup decision over the next few weeks could be the difference between making the postseason and watching from the sideline.

There's no time to sit around waiting for players to figure it out. We need production, and we need it now.

Let's get into the Week 12 Panic Meter.

Kenneth Walker III, RB, Kansas City Chiefs

Panic level: No Panic

I know the noise around Kenneth Walker III is loud right now. Rookie Emmett Johnson has been sensational in the games Walker has missed, and fantasy managers are wondering if we're witnessing a changing of the guard in Kansas City.

The word out of Kansas City on Monday, via Eric Bieniemy, is that Walker remains the starter when he's available. When K9 is on the field, K9 is the lead ball-carrier in this offense.

That "when he's available" part matters, though. Walker has been ruled out for the third straight game on Thursday night against the Bills due to a groin injury.

Here's what I will say: Johnson has earned a meaningful role in this offense. Think of him as a souped-up, "Super Saiyan" version of Jerick McKinnon. He deserves to be on the field, and his involvement shouldn't disappear when Walker returns. I can absolutely see Johnson settling into an 8-to-12-touch-per-game role, which could take something off Walker's ceiling.

But the way this Chiefs offense is humming right now, both on the ground and through the air, there's room for both backs to be productive. When Walker gets healthy, this has a chance to be one of the best backfields in the NFL, if not THE best.

If Walker is healthy and active, he's in your lineup. Don't let Johnson's emergence talk you out of starting K9. Also, don't let Walker being active deter you from flexing Johnson. 

Emeka Egbuka, WR, Tampa Bay Buccaneers

Panic level: No Panic (for me)/Total Panic (if you're still a believer)

Emeka Egbuka has now gone 16 consecutive appearances without reaching 65 receiving yards, dating back to last season. He's seen five targets in each of his last two games, totaling 56 receiving yards. Meanwhile, rookie Ted Hurst III just found the end zone twice for Tampa Bay.

This is a far cry from the receiver who lit up the first half of his rookie season.

So why am I not panicking? Because I've already adjusted my expectations. Egbuka isn't a WR1 or even a high-end WR2 at this point. He's a WR3 with the potential to deliver WR2 or WR1 production in any given week. If that's how you're valuing him, nothing from Week 11 should shock you.

No panic doesn't mean he's a must-start. He's a WR3 or flex option, and there are going to be weeks when you have better options on your roster.

Now, if you're still holding onto the version of Egbuka we saw during the first half of his rookie year, you should be in total panic territory.

Sixteen appearances isn't a slump anymore. That's who he's been.

Trey McBride, TE, Arizona Cardinals

Panic level: Some Panic (bordering on Total)

Trey McBride probably belongs in total panic territory, but the sheer volume of opportunities he's getting makes it difficult to put him there.

The Cardinals are down to their fourth-string quarterback in journeyman Josh Johnson. There was legitimate concern about what that would look like against Kansas City on Sunday, but McBride still managed to draw a season-high 14 targets, turning them into nine receptions for 54 yards.

Fourteen targets for 54 yards. That's where the concern lies.

There isn't much happening downfield for McBride in this version of the Arizona offense. It's to get the ball in his hands as quickly as possible and hope he can make something happen after the catch. Touchdown opportunities are going to be difficult to come by, and the Cardinals still haven't settled on who will start at quarterback moving forward.

The volume is enough to keep McBride in your lineup, but expecting him to provide the type of positional advantage we've become accustomed to is probably unrealistic right now.

Close to total panic? Absolutely. Am I recommending that you bench Trey McBride in a 1-TE league? No.

Garrett Wilson, WR, New York Jets

Panic level: Some Panic

It wouldn't be a Panic Meter without a New York Jets player, and unfortunately, we have to talk about Garrett Wilson once again.

At the start of the year, I thought this would be the season Wilson finally got north of 15 half-PPR points per game. Instead, we're looking at another season in that 13-14-point-per-game range.

This isn't a talent issue. We may have seen the best version of the Jets offense on Sunday, and that's exactly the problem for Wilson's fantasy outlook.

Breece Hall and Braelon Allen combined for 36 carries and 161 rushing yards. Geno Smith was incredibly efficient when asked to throw the football, completing 17-of-21 passes with three touchdowns and no interceptions. Wilson played 90% of the offensive snaps and was still the team's leading receiver.

Wilson's involvement isn't the issue. There just aren't enough passing opportunities when the Jets are leaning on what I consider one of the best 1-2 punches at running back in the NFL.

If the Jets can run the football effectively, limit what they're asking Geno to do and capitalize on his passing opportunities, why would they change that?

It works for the Jets. It caps Wilson.

He's still an every-week fantasy starter for most managers, but he's a WR2 with upside rather than the high-end WR1 many of us hoped he would become this season.

Indianapolis Colts offense (Jonathan Taylor, Tyler Warren)

Panic level: Coping Corner

After sleepwalking through much of the season, the Indianapolis Colts finally did what a lot of fantasy managers wanted to do weeks ago. They'd had enough of Daniel Jones, released him and handed the keys to Anthony Richardson Sr.

Does that make this offense better? Probably not.

Richardson hasn't proven that he's the answer to the Colts' passing game, and he's stepping into an offense that's already without two important pieces.

No Josh Downs. No Quenton Nelson. No Daniel Jones. No problem, right?

Where things could improve is in the running game. Richardson's ability to keep the football on read-option plays gives opposing defenses something else to account for and could open up rushing lanes for Jonathan Taylor. Of course, that same rushing ability could also cost Taylor carries and touchdown opportunities around the goal line.

Taylor and Tyler Warren aren't necessarily in the same situation, though.

Taylor's workload had been declining as rookie Seth McGowan earned more opportunities. McGowan's hamstring injury could push some of that volume back in Taylor's direction, although we don't have a clear timeline for McGowan's return.

JT has been borderline unplayable lately and continues to slide down my weekly rankings. There is at least a realistic path for him to get back on track if the volume returns and Richardson's presence helps the rushing attack.

It's much more difficult to see that path for Warren. In four games since returning from injury, Warren has caught 11 of 25 targets for 85 yards.

Maybe Richardson has been sitting on the bench all this time thinking, "When I get my opportunity, I've got to get the ball to Tyler Warren."

That's blind hope, faith and optimism at this point.

Warren is going to be outside my top-15 tight ends for Week 12. If there's a dependable option on your bench or somebody available on the waiver wire, make that move.

A quarterback change doesn't automatically fix a bad offense. Taylor has a path back to fantasy relevance through volume, but neither player deserves automatic consideration in your starting lineup right now.

Welcome to the Coping Corner, Indianapolis.

item.description: Congratulations to Jonah Coleman for his first AFC Offensive Player of the Week award for his 24 carry, 111 yard and three touchdown day against the Las Vegas Raiders.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos made a switch at running back on Sunday against the Las Vegas Raiders that ultimately paid massive dividends. With J.K. Dobbins relegated to a single snap, rookie Jonah Coleman officially took the reins in Denver’s run game. The result? 129 total yards and three touchdowns.

That effort earn Coleman his first ever AFC Offensive Player of the Week award.

He joins 11 other Broncos’ running backs to have won this award over the years, but only two have every won it multiple times (C.J. Anderson twice, Terrell Davis three times).

Coleman finished with 24 carries for 111 yards and three touchdowns and also added another four receptions for 18 yards. His snap counts have grown from around 50-50 split with Dobbins to 66%, then 77%, to 85% in each of the last three games. The switch to Coleman as the primary running back in Denver is complete.

The move made sense from a production standpoint too. He is averaging 4.3 yards per carry to 3.3 from Dobbins. When RJ Harvey returns — maybe as soon as next week — the one-two punch from these two on the field could be just what the doctor ordered for this Broncos’ offense down the stretch.

Let’s give a Mile High Salute to Jonah Coleman!

My daughter retired from the military at the start of the season and came home to start her civilian life. We love having her back. Our sons are excited to hang out with their big sister. My wife and I get an extra driver for the boys. Win-win.

Well, until we started talking about the Thanksgiving menu.

She hasn't been home for the holidays in the better part of a decade, so we're pulling out all the stops for Thursday. I'll have at least two types of meat in the smoker. Multiple veggie dishes. Not to mention the family members coming over to spend time at the new house. Between Wednesday's game, the Thursday triple-header and a Black Friday special, I'll probably get roped into so many conversations I'll only be able to watch the game in pieces.

If your situation is anything like mine, here's one thing I'll be watching for in each game. If that's all you've got time to check before food's ready, you'll know what matters for your fantasy football lineups.

Can 'Love Find Its Rhythm' Again?

I'm glad Green Bay got an extra week to reset after going up against the Vikings. Unlike Brock Purdy and the 49ers, Jordan Love didn't fare so well.

Harrison Smith picks it off in the end zone!

MINvsGB on FOX/FOX One
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/4FyAQkSdGU

— NFL (@NFL) November 15, 2026

To be fair, Love isn't the first to fall victim to DC Brian Flores' unit. Purdy is the only QB whose efficiency metrics improve with a bunch of purple in front of him. But what might be more concerning for the Packers is if the slump lingers into the next game. Because it wouldn't be the first time. 

Five of the seven QBs with a game before and after facing Minnesota posted a lower EPA per dropback in their next game than their average before the matchup. Of course, you can poke holes in the narrative I'm suggesting. Daniel Jones, Tyler Shough and Malik Willis aren't world beaters. But Josh Allen posted his first game under 200 passing yards after getting pummeled by Minnesota in primetime (10 hits, season-high). Jared Goff was an outright disaster in Miami, notching his first game of '26 without a passing TD and his third with three or more sacks. Again, this is why the Packers bye couldn't have come at a better time, as the Rams have their own way of creating havoc for enemy QBs.

This Myles Garrett-Aaron Donald pairing is gonna be cinema the rest of the year.

Also, look how happy every DL is that Donald got his first sack. pic.twitter.com/Vyr4yx9nhC

— Sosa Kremenjas (@QBsMVP) November 16, 2026

Week 10 was just the second game where L.A. could feature the vaunted duo of Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald. Turning them loose against the Commanders and Cardinals seems like some sort of crime. But it paints a similar picture to Love's environment the last time we saw him.

  • Time to Pressure (Weeks 10-11): 2.2, T-1st 

  • Sack Rate: 17.0%, 4th

  • Blitz Rate: 26.2%, 17th 

The Rams put QBs in a bind, but not by sending the house on seemingly every snap. In their two games together, Garrett and Donald have combined for 14 quick pressures. Braden Fiske and Byron Young have four each, too. Meanwhile, on the backend, their secondary has allowed just four TDs over a six-game stretch. They're especially stingy on intermediate throws, giving up three or fewer receptions on attempts of that depth in all but one game.

Josh Jacobs is still recovering. The offense will have to rely on Love's shoulder yet again. So, if you look up and see him struggling to connect with his receivers, or Matthew Golden having another ill-timed drop, just hope one connects for a TD and we can move on to Week 12.

Can the Bears Tame the Lions?

I talked about Chicago's lackluster start to the second half of their season on Sunday. In truth, the Bears defense was the real MVP. The runner-up was the Saints' first-quarter offense. They've scored a total of nine points in the first 15 minutes in 2026. But after Chicago mounted a multi-score lead, Tyler Shough found a rhythm.

  • Drive #4: 7 (Plays), 80 (Net Yards), 3:47 (Drive Time)

  • Drive #6: 9, 46, 0:54

  • Drive #8: 12, 37, 5:49

  • Drive #10: 9, 44, 4:05

  • Drive #11: 14, 47, 3:48

Now, on the one hand, just three of these drives turned into points for New Orleans. And only one resulted in a TD. But look at the number of plays run and the time Caleb Williams had to spend on the bench. Surprisingly, Chicago generated just one more first down on offense than the Saints (18 to 17). Its defensive success rate (57.7%) was actually worse than the Saints' (60.3%). If Shough could do that, think about what the Bears' upcoming opponent will do.

WAYMOOOOOO 57-YARDER pic.twitter.com/YcSKTBYX73

— Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 22, 2026

Jared Goff blacked out against the Bucs. HC Todd Bowles blitzed him on 36.7% of his dropbacks. Goff didn't even take a sack while completing 7 of 11 attempts. Tampa's defensive front put Goff under duress 43.3% of the time, and that didn't faze him either. In fact, Sunday afternoon, given the stakes, was Goff's best performance when pressured since coming to Detroit.

  • Success Rate (when pressured): 58.3%, Highest (of 17 games with +40% pressure rate)

  • EPA per Dropback: 0.45, 2nd 

  • Pressure-to-Sack Ratio: 7.7%, 4th-lowest 

OC Drew Petzing's game plan was perfect. They attacked the seams of the Bucs' zone coverage for multiple chunk gains. With Jahmyr Gibbs stepping up to block DT Vita Vea, the Lions could flood the exterior of the defensive coverage with four receivers out on a route (2 WRs, 2 TEs) on 28.6% of Goff's dropbacks. Or, as the above clip highlights, he could beat them the old-fashioned way with Jameson Williams.

Chicago just let the Saints dink-and-dunk their way into a close game. And the Lions can play that way, too. But the explosive element always lies in wait. So, if the Bears stall on either side of the ball, the Lions can pounce on them and maintain their lead in the NFC North.

Is Joe Milton for Real?

I didn't turn on the PIT-PHI game until late in the fourth quarter. My thought was Pittsburgh would pull out the win, and the race in the AFC North would stay close. But on just 21 passing attempts, Joe Milton got his first win as a starting QB. But it wasn't all pretty.

Thank goodness Joe Milton is so bad #Steelerspic.twitter.com/RXWGMVc1eB

— Steelers Depot 7⃣ (@Steelersdepot) November 22, 2026

To say the Eagles are trying to ease Milton into the role (i.e., hiding their passing game) would be kind. Philadelphia went from a -1.1% PROE in his first start, had the bye week to plan and came out throwing even less (-10.6%). Don't get me wrong — Milton didn't acquit himself of any poor play. He ranked second-worst and fifth-worst, respectively, in CPOE across both starts. Somehow, at 6-foot-5, 246 pounds, Milton is averaging five sacks a game. Luckily, he's using his speed as a runner (3.6 FPPG on the ground), but the arm talent could use a boost.

Enter Dallas' defense.

Only three QBs have squared off with the Cowboys and not walked away with one of their best efficiency marks of the season. Dallas even switched defensive play-callers, and it was still in the bottom 10 in defensive success rate. Admittedly, Cam Ward's TDs were unethical at best. But as a Bengals fan, expecting your offense to score 30+ is akin to thinking hope is a plan. However, with DeVonta Smith back, Dak Prescott might need to do just that.

All-22 view of Milton’s missed bomb to DeVonta Smith. Overthrow or catchable? pic.twitter.com/CtyWmv5cyF

— Victor Williams (@ThePhillyPod) November 23, 2026

Outside of Smith coming back to a laughable 57.1% target share, he also took 61.1% of the air yards. Milton tried him on throws of 25 and 53 air yards, but the two couldn't quite hook up. If I see that on Thursday, we're in for a wild ride on Thanksgiving. 

The Bill Comes Due

The Chiefs have two problems, and one of them won’t be solved on Thursday. Well, honestly, the issues belong to us fantasy managers. But Kansas City's offense does have something of a dilemma on its hands.

Emmett Johnson has now recorded back to back 100 yard rushing games since taking over for Kenneth Walker.

23 CAR, 105 RUSH YDS, 1 TD, 4 REC, 38 REC YDS vs Cardinals.

Johnson's OROY chances have skyrocketed over the last two weeks. https://t.co/dt5FdKVwLipic.twitter.com/tNep8zsuxb

— Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) November 22, 2026

Watching Emmett Johnson come in relief of Kenneth Walker III has been great for both the Chiefs and fantasy managers. Nothing changed about how they do business. HC Andy Reid only opted to run on 46.7% of their early-down plays, but Johnson gained four or more yards on 53.8% of those carries. From a utilization standpoint, Walker and Johnson look interchangeable. 

  • Early-Down Rushing Share: 79.1% (Walker W1-9), 81.3% (Johnson W10-11)

  • Route Rate: 45.3%, 76.9%

  • Target Share: 14.6%, 15.7%

But something has to give. Walker is set to miss another game in Week 12 due to his groin injury. When both were healthy, the Chiefs ran six plays with both on the field. Mahomes is already averaging the 12th-most dropbacks per game, so there's little chance of Kansas City becoming a rushing team. However, if there's one area where the two RBs could split the workload, it's in the passing game. But that will have to wait at least another game.

  • Yards per Route Run (as the starter): 1.80 (Johnson), 1.31 (Walker)

  • YAC per Reception: 14.0, 7.7

It should be no surprise that the younger, faster rookie can churn out more yards with the ball in his hands and a clear runway. However, the Chiefs' passing game has its own concerns. 

I realize I'm going to come off as a Chiefs' hater, but the last two weeks have been preseason games for Patrick Mahomes. The last time he threw for more than 300 yards in back-to-back games was in 2023. Sure, the offensive line is still an issue, but his hits and sacks have been down, too. And the timing couldn't be better, as it's allowed him to find the best ways to use his receivers. 

Reid hasn't unleashed Josh Downs yet. He was up to a 32.5% route share and five targets after making a splash in his debut. The good news for gamers rostering Downs is that when he was on the field, Mahomes was looking for him. His 38.5% TPRR led the Chiefs' pass-catchers. The downside is that on the eight routes that Downs wasn't the primary target, Mahomes was making magic with the other receivers.

The above clip highlights how No. 15 used Downs' gravity to pull defenders to the sticks, leaving space for Rashee Rice. Two plays later, instead of going to the intermediate part of the field again, Mahomes hits Johnson on a screen to set up an easy 4th and 1. The deep shots to Xavier Worthy or Cyrus Allen didn't always work, but the tendency to look 15+ air yards downfield hasn't been an element of the Chiefs' passing game for a while. And if Week 11 was any indication, Kansas City went from having limited reliable receivers to multiple.

  • Travis Kelce: 18.9% (Target Rate)

  • Rashee Rice: 16.2%

  • Noah Gray: 13.5%

  • Josh Downs: 13.5%

  • Xavier Worthy: 10.8%

  • Cyrus Allen: 10.8%

  • Emmett Johnson: 10.8%

In Week 10, six different pass-catchers earned three or more targets. That was up to seven against the Cardinals. Mahomes ranked 2nd and 9th in PROE in those games, respectively, but without a clear WR1, we're hoping someone other than the RBs gets into the end zone. That should change on Thursday night.

Buffalo is first in offensive PPG and fourth in YPG. The Chiefs shouldn't have time to test things out or see what works best. Playoff seeding is on the line. So, I'll be seeing which pass-catchers become Mahomes' top options in one of the biggest games of the regular season.

Coleman's Black Friday Doorbuster

I believed Jonah Coleman would take over the backfield in Denver. But I've been waiting for HC Sean Payton to do what he's done for years: split the backfield. Through the first six weeks, J.K. Dobbins played on 54.8% of the early-down snaps. But he was mostly off the field on third downs. Tyler Badie and RJ Harvey handled 77.8% of the RB touches in obvious passing situations. And everybody got the ball in the red zone. But maybe the rookie has made Payton change his ways.

Jonah Coleman entered Sunday with just 80 rushing yards this season before breaking out against Las Vegas.

24 CAR, 111 RUSH YDS, 3 TD, 4 REC, 18 REC YDS vs Raiders.

Denver has now won six straight games and is looking like a legitimate Super Bowl contender. https://t.co/ihXa9lXCBfpic.twitter.com/LaonzcDicB

— Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) November 23, 2026

Thinking back on it, if there were ever a matchup for Coleman to take advantage of, it'd be against the Raiders. Their run defense was allowing a whopping 131.9 YPG to opposing RBs. And to make matters worse, the short-area coverage ranked 32nd in completion rate to rushers (91.7%). Essentially, any way that someone out of Denver's backfield got the ball, they'd turn it into a positive result. I just didn't think so many of those touches would go to Coleman.

  • Rushing Rate: 88.9%

  • Target Share: 13.0%

  • Short-Yardage Snap Rate: 100.0%

Going back to my thoughts on Payton's tendencies, how often he turned to Coleman isn't something we can wave away. His 88.9% share of the carries is the most of any running back since Payton came to Denver in '23. Third downs? All Coleman. Targets to RBs? 100.0% to Coleman.

I have no doubt we'll see No. 20 start the game. But I'll be watching for his workload. And if we don't see any more Payton backfield hijinks, Coleman will have the OROY award locked up before the stores close.
